The hon. member asked what effect the extra energy costs will have on food prices for consumers. We have carried out some research which indicates that if we went to world prices for energy immediately, by 1985 food price increases to consumers will be as high as 35 to 40 per cent for that one reason alone.
Farmers face the same energy crises as other businesses. The 1980 prices for petroleum products paid by farmers increased by 17 per cent. Earlier the member for Elgin asked about energy costs. I was glad to hear the member for Algoma point out the savings in the period ending 1984 amounting to $8,220. I might point out it is not uncommon for farms to use 6,000 gallons per year. The hon. member for Elgin asked what kind of cushion we were providing. I say that is a pretty good cushion compared to what the Crosbie budget would have offered. We said we would attempt to cushion the rise in energy costs, and that is not a bad cushion.
There are other programs as well. Research is being carried out on renewable energy, biomass materials, the production of gasohol and alcohol from grain products. At the present time that appears to be uneconomic if other sources of energy are used to produce it, such as oil, stove oil, bunker oil, furnace oil or natural gas. If solar energy is used, there is some potential. The same applies to burning off gas, which is not presently being done.
Minimum research, or possibly more than that, has been carried out on farm tillage-for example, how much should be used on western grain farms. Fuel requirements can be reduced under proper conditions by over 30 per cent compared with conventional tillage practices. We know there are many areas where this can be done. Under the program announced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, we will be working very closely with his department on a national energy saving program for food and food processing. By working in many small ways, it can add up to a significant saving.
I would also point out that in the food sector there has been a saving of 15 per cent in a little less than two years. That is an amazing feat of energy conservation. We see savings in farming come about through improved farm machinery, motor vehicle maintenance, and the use of low temperature crop drying systems. A farmer in my area, the former chairman of the Soybean Marketing Board, has invented a unique grain drying system, probably the most unique in southern Ontario, which does not use gas or oil for drying. It has been viewed by people from as far away as China. He gets a premium on this grain because it is naturally dried grain. Usually the only system he uses is air but on some occasions he uses electric heat bulbs. It is one of the most unique systems of all. There can be a tremendous saving on grain drying using this type of system.
In livestock production fuel consumption is being cut by improved insulation, ventilation, by the recovery of heat from
Supply
exhaust air, by controlling livestock housing temperatures in heated buildings, and in other ways. Much feel has been wasted in the past. We are very proud of some of the things people are accomplishing with all the conservation demonstration projects on many farms in different parts of Canada. Funds for these projects have been provided by the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Resources. We do not know how successful some of these will be, but the ingenuity and the initiative taken by some of the producers in coming up with new ways and new ideas to save energy are utterly fantastic.

Mr. Chairman, I asked the minister if he had an actual indication of the amount of funding provided to Saskatchewan, Manitoba and to northwestern Ontario for drought relief assistance in the past year. Does the minister have an actual figure on the cost of that assistance?

Yes, we do have the figures. In the first instance we said we would pay $7 million for transportation of forage into northern Ontario, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Those funds were not all used. We then announced we would use moneys for herd maintenance programs. We said we would use over $60 million. I do not have the actual amounts of money paid out because it is not finalized. It appears we would be paying out a total of possibly $67 million or maybe a little less.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The parties have advised me that an agreement has been reached to permit any party, and in this particular case the NDP, to subdivide the 20-minute period into two ten-minute periods each. In order to do that it would require unanimous consent of the House. The parties have advised me there is unanimous consent of the House. Is that agreed?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few minutes to make some remarks and go over some questions that the minister has been asked. I realize the importance of agriculture in our economy. I listened carefully to some speeches that were made yesterday by members of my province. In fact, from time to time we probably share the same interests and the same problems when we speak of Quebec and agricultural measures.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to tell the minister at the outset that I will probably be less aggressive than I was five years ago when several of my colleagues shared my preoccupations and those of farmers, particularly in the dairy industry in Quebec. Yesterday, the parliamentary secretary explained the background of the agricultural development in Quebec and his comments about the direction of agriculture in Quebec and the rest of Canada were interesting and useful.
Still I would like to refer to the document that all members have received and question the minister, given the interest also shown by farmers in my riding, not to mention milk producers, potato producers, tobacco producers and horticulturists. So

December 10, 1980
Supply
agriculture plays an important part in the economy of my riding.
Many farmers are concerned about their future and they have made it known in the brief presented recently by the dairy farmers of Canada to the minister and the department. Yesterday the member for Champlain, 1 think, talked about a rumour to the effect that the government was intent on putting an end to these subsidies of $2.66 and the minister said that he was not aware of any such recommendation. I would have preferred him to say that no such measure was being considered and that milk producers would continue receiving these subsidies.
The minister said a few times since the beginning of this debate that he regretted not having time to give answers. I am going to try to give him time to answer for the official record. He may rest assured, Mr. Chairman, that I will convey his answers to the farmers of my riding and that Quebec farmers will also be interested to learn about them.
Could the minister tell us right now if these subsidies to dairy producers are not going to be maintained?

Mr. Chairman, I have told two hon. members today, one during the question period and just recently the member for Algoma, there is no truth to that whatsoever. The Treasury Board has approved the program as of Monday this week for this coming year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister for his reply.
The dairy farmers of Canada are also concerned. In 1975, the federal government announced the implementation of a policy to increase prices comprising a formula for adjusting the income of producers to production costs.
Can the minister tell us today whether or not this policy will be maintained over the long term, since the dairy farmers of Canada stress the importance for the government to commit itself to helping producers over the long haul? Can the minister assure dairy producers that formula pricing will be maintained? For how many years will it apply? I am not sure I can put the question to him in those words, but it does seem that the dairy farmers stress the need for a long-term commitment in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, if only all agricultural producers in the world had been served as well as the dairy producers have been served under the Canadian dairy policy. 1 know of no other group of dairy producers in the world who have the kind of long-term dairy policy Canadian producers enjoy. It is one which has been there for many years. It is reviewed every year and unless there is going to be some drastic change they would be notified in due time. There is no suggestion by the dairy producers or by the government at this
time that there be any kind of change. It is under review. It is an agreement we made when we established the long-term dairy policy that it would be reviewed from time to time and that is being done at the present time. They would have to go over all the workings and ramifications of this dairy policy. Almost everyone who examines the dairy program run by the dairy commission is complimentary.
We have had people from Japan, from France, from Switzerland, from West Germany come to see this program which is managed so well. I think we are the envy of the world. In practically every other part of the world where dairy production is of any significance there are problems which supersede ours. They are mismanaged in every way imaginable. Even Japan has dairy surpluses and does not know what to do with them. Ours is the best managed of any dairy program in the entire world.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has said time and time again that Canada has the best system in the world. I am not in the mood to discuss that at this time; I am merely concerned with the interests of the dairy farmers of Canada. His colleagues, I am sure, agree with me and would like to know whether or not the government intends to maintain the formula pricing. I do not want the minister to tell me again that he has the best system in the world. We know things are working out reasonably well at this time. I merely want to know, for the benefit of the dairy farmers of Canada, which comprises all dairy producers in the country, whether the government intends to keep the formula. The minister did say "unless there is going to be some drastic change" so right away dairy farmers worry. So, I would like him to tell us whether or not formula pricing will be in effect for one, two or three years. That is the question of the dairy farmers of Canada; it is not mine, Mr. Minister.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows, formula pricing has been here since 1975. I do not know if the hon. member is trying to create discontent, trying to start a rumour or what have you, but no one has suggested that formula pricing should be changed, not this minister nor any other minister in this government, as far as I know. There has been no suggestion that formula pricing be changed.
People in other parts of our society have a much more fixed situation than do the dairy farmers of Canada. When we give them formula pricing, it is not any greater than in many other parts of our productive society, nor even some parts of our society which are not so productive with respect to indexing the cost of living for senior citizens, people on disability pensions and others. The formula pricing we have for our dairy farmers is better than that in any other part of the world. The hon. member asked me not to repeat that, but I do so because other parts of the world do not have such a good system for their dairy farmers.
December 10, 1980

Mr. Chairman, I can appreciate that the minister would give me the same reply as earlier. I do not want to alarm the producers or the Canadian population. My question is very simple. The dairy farmers of Canada hope and wish the minister will maintain this formula pricing. They said so, as the minister is well aware. 1 simply wanted to ask the minister if he could tell me what he will be able to do for them. Will he maintain this formula pricing this year, at least for some time? 1 do not know. However, I believe the minister could tell me.
1 know that this formula has had good results since 1975. I know all that, but dairy farmers would like to know whether the minister can guarantee that this formula will be maintained and for how long, or at least, I imagine that they would like to be reassured that this formula will still be applied in 1981. If the minister can provide further reassurance, so much the better for dairy farmers. In other words, I am asking the same question once again. Can the minister tell us whether this formula will be maintained in 1981?
Mr. Chairman, yes.

This reply is very satisfactory, Mr. Chairman. I really like a minister who can provide such answers. I would like to note, Mr. Chairman, that after the contribution made by certain members yesterday, I also had the opportunity to ask certain questions of the minister about the subsidy for pork producers, who include pig fatteners and weaner pig producers. One of the members, I do not remember which one, either the member for Champlain or the member for Chicoutimi, mentioned the delays in receiving these subsidies. I do not want to ask any question of the minister about this, but 1 simply want to say that I have also received complaints in this regard and I imagine that, after hearing the comments made by my colleagues opposite, the minister will take some action to try to reduce the waiting period for pork producers as concerns the subsidies. Of course, 1 am happy that the minister has reacted to the representations made concerning the situation of pork producers.
There is another question I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, Mr. Chairman. I have read today in the newspaper that there is a surplus of maple syrup. Perhaps maple syrup producers would be interested in learning whether the minister is aware of this surplus, which is of particular concern to Quebec, as it seems that it could mean losses for producers who would have to store surplus syrup. Moreover, according to the international institute, there seems to be a budget problem for promoting maple syrup. Could the minister throw some light on the subject today?
Is the department prepared to increase allocations for promoting maple syrup? Could the minister tell us whether he
Supply
would be willing to recommend a moderate budget for promotional purposes so that the producers and the association can dispose of this surplus and also of the maple syrup production they will have in a few months? Perhaps the minister could throw some light on the situation for the information of maple syrup producers.
For the moment, the one who is wasting the time of the House is the minister. He is robbing me of my allotted time.

Mr. Chairman, we are aware that producers in la belle province had a very good crop of maple syrup last year. We are trying to find figures for the hon. member, but we give producers interest-free advance payments for their maple syrup so that they can properly supply the market. I am not aware whether there is a problem at the present time in marketing the product. I understand it was of high quality. It was on the market at a fairly good price. We advance the moneys so that the producers do not have to sell their product in a distressed market, so that the product does not have to seek a home on the market and so that speculators are not able to take advantage of the maple syrup producers.
We do not have the figure in front of us at this time, but 1 have received no representations from maple syrup producers in the last few months to my knowledge, so I am taking for granted that things are going as they had projected and hoped. If the hon. member has any information which is contrary to that, I would be pleased to have it, but I have not received any representations along those lines from the official organization representing maple syrup producers.

Mr. Chairman, according to a press release I have here from the International Institute of Maple Syrup Producers-which the parliamentary secretary will no doubt provide him with-there is four times more maple syrup than usual for this time. Under the circumstances, it seems to me that that surplus creates a problem. Perhaps we should consider an advertising campaign and perhaps the minister could ask his officials to look into the possibility of selling a part of this maple syrup outside the country.
But my time is going fast, Mr. Chairman, and I also want to voice to the minister my main concern regarding this sector and that is the question of younger producers who are expected to carry on. We must recognize that this industry is healthier today than before and we have reason to be optimistic, but we must also recognize, as others have indicated, that considering the cost of farms, it is difficult nowadays, even though the lending facilities are there, for a young would-be farmer to buy a farm because of the interest rate, which is also true for other areas. Interest rates represent a prohibitive cost and jeopardize the future of farming for the younger generations. They can also discourage the young from going into debt because there are years when production is not so good. I do not have any solutions to propose to the minister but I would ask him to

December 10, 1980
Supply
consider seriously this concern by young producers, this reluctance on their part to go into debt to buy a family farm.
Today, because of their cost, farms are often sold to foreign interests. There has been a change in outlook and values such that the children have a harder time maintaining the family farm, because of cost and interest rates. The minister could therefore consider implementing a specific policy to help young producers become owners and keep the family farm, a policy dealing with these interest costs which are a terrible handicap for the young who are interested in farming.
The minister is perfectly aware of the long-term situation, in any case, and 1 think that here and now we must concern ourselves with the interest cost problems those young people will have. I could raise the same concerns about the present situation of small home owners. The industry itself is concerned. The subject being agriculture, let us not stray from it. I try to be very objective in my approach, Mr. Chairman, because those are comments we often hear from young farmers who are wondering where the obligation to borrow sums of $150,000 or $200,000 is leading us. At the same time, we cannot help but think that that will indirectly affect production costs, and consequently, the consumer will be directly affected. In the circumstances, I take this opportunity to invite the minister to consider seriously this problem and the future of our young people in agriculture. It is important that young people get increasingly more interested. Some are interested, but the opportunities are limited and right now, in view of the present economic difficulties we all know about, I think interest rates weigh heavily on the future of agriculture. I ask the minister to give the matter serious consideration and try in any case to bring forward a policy that will encourage young Canadians and help them choose agriculture.
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether I have a few more minutes-
One minute.

I have one minute left. I shall give that last minute to the dear minister who has too often complained he did not have enough time to answer. I hope he will seriously consider that last point 1 made, assistance to young farmers, the commitment to them, and funding is the way. I understand the minister's difficulties, but would he also understand the problems those young people face?

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say that in different parts of Canada there are different kinds of agricultural production, but in la belle province, from which the hon. member comes, the production entity is there. There is only one which I can think of, perhaps two, which does not have some kind of cost-pricing formula. For every dairy farmer who wants to sell out in Quebec, there are three young farmers who
want to enter the business, and they are protected with the cost-price formula for interest rates, etc. There is a subsidized form of interest rates for young farmers in Quebec.
To put the record straight, Mr. Chairman, let me say that we have more young farmers percentagewise in the business. The average age of young farmers entering agriculture is the highest since 1951, if I remember the figures correctly. I do not have the exact percentages but there are more young farmers in agriculture now than many people realize. Those are people who have graduated from agricultural schools and university agricultural courses. We have a higher percentage of those young people entering agriculture now because of the good programs we have established for them.

Mr. Chairman, first I want to make a couple of comments, and then I will put my questions on a particular area.
Several times in the last three days I have heard it said that 20 years ago one farmer could feed 30 people. Now one farmer feeds 55 people and 20 years from now one farmer will feed 200 people. I am concerned about that approach because the implication is that farmers are becoming more efficient and productive. Possibly they are on an individual basis, but not a great deal more food is being produced per acre of land. I just wanted to make that comment to start with. I think we should watch what is happening so that we do not push too many of our farmers off the land, saying we have very efficient farmers because one farmer can feed 200 people.
Last year has not been a particularly good year for farmers. In the west we started out with a drought which lasted, in certain parts of the west, until the fall and which affected hay crops in particular. The result was that farmers did not have the kind of feed available to them that they had expected. Also, it pushed up the price of hay for feed in the west considerably, in some cases to twice the price it had been the previous year. Also, prices increased for other products and equipment, as was well documented at the Outlook conference last week. The price of fertilizer increased by 15 per cent. I am using ballpark figures because I did not take note of the exact figures which were given. Fuel and fuel-related costs increased by as much as 20 per cent to 24 per cent, depending on what was included in that category. Wages increased by 10 per cent, machinery increased by approximately 15 per cent, interest costs increased by about 20 per cent, and farm land, depending on the location, increased from 20 per cent to 50 per cent.
The effect of those increases was that the real income of farmers in the last year was reduced by 3 per cent. Actually, the reduction is greater than that because that included a certain reduction of inventory as well. We should put these increases in costs against the income of the farmer. The price of grain has gone up in the last little while but, owing to lack of attention on the part of the present government and the former Conservative government, the actual income to farmers from grain was considerably reduced. Also, the price of beef has not increased sufficiently to cover the cost of production, and the price of hogs dropped considerably.
December 10, 1980

On the whole, farmers have not been doing particularly well in the last year, although the Minister of Agriculture often says that he is in favour of orderly marketing, we cannot be quite sure of that. We seem to go to the free market and every time we do it does the farmer harm. For example, let us consider the embargo. If we had gone to world markets during the time of the embargo, the income of farmers from grain would have increased by a considerable amount in the last year. However, the embargo was imposed.
The principle of compensation for losses suffered by farmers as a result of the embargo has been established by the Conservative government and the Liberal government, and the Prime Minister even made a statement in that regard. Since the spring the government has been working on compensation studies. The minister said that the compensation document would be ready by the end of November, and November has long gone. I am just wondering what is the status of that document. Does the minister have any sense of urgency in this matter? I have referred the fact that costs have increased and incomes have gone down, partly because of the embargo maintained by the government.
On August 23 the minister reponsible for fitness and amateur sport announced that Canadian athletes who were barred from competing in the Moscow Olympics would receive:
-a program of assistance that will facilitate their further education, as well as the development of alternative career possibilities ... The assistance intended will take the form of actual tuition fees pursuant to normal Canadian standards and related educational support of up to $200 per month during the academic year.
That commitment was specific. It indicated the level of support and delivered on the promise which the federal government made to the athletes of Canada. If the government can do this for the athletes, can it not do it for farmers by naming the crops to be covered and the range of compensation in dollars, so that farmers can make their plans, knowing the specific period of time they can expect that compensation? Can the minister give those specific undertakings now? I will give him an opportunity to answer before my ten minutes are up.
A lot of studies are being conducted, but I should like to ask the minister some questions dealing with the embargo. When will we hear about the embargo? How much will the compensation be? How did they arrive at the figures? If those figures are not adequate, may farm organizations make submissions to the minister in order to give their understanding of what compensation should be paid?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member talked about the incomes of farmers being down. We recognize that, and 1 have stated that. Their net incomes are down 3 per cent, but they are still in a very substantial net position. Also he talked about the price of beef not being high enough. Of course, the over-all production of pork had a depressing effect upon the price of beef, poultry products and every other meat product. Pork was sold on the market below the cost of production. It
Supply
was distress selling and the sale prices had the effect to which I refer.
Also the member referred to the embargo and to compensation to farmers who may have lost income because of the embargo. The embargo was put in place by the previous government. The document which I hoped would be finished by the end of November is now ready for signing. It will be signed and submitted to cabinet for consideration in the next two or three days. I cannot tell the hon. member what the document indicates until it has been seen and considered by cabinet. As far as I am concerned, we intend to live up to what we have said. As I said the other day in the House, we do not intend to welsh on any agreement made by the previous government; this is one we said we would fulfil.

Mr. Chairman, I will hurriedly dash through my comments in order that the minister might respond. I am really looking for some support from the minister for the farm machinery industry. Those of us who are concerned about the health of the farm machinery industry well appreciate the difficulties of farmers at the moment in even replacing their machinery as this becomes necessary.
I had occasion to look at some of the statistics which have come out in recent months. The most recent were released last Monday and showed quite clearly that farm income is not keeping pace with inflation. In 1979 the cash receipts of farmers were $14.1 billion. In 1980 they had risen to $15.3 billion. Unfortunately they do not afford farmers the opportunity to maintain equality with their 1979 position. In 1979 the net real income of farmers was $3.61 billion, but in 1980 it was only $3.49 billion. In 1979 the interest on the debt load, which includes the debt load on land, was $1.33 billion, but by 1980 it had risen to $1.5 billion.
I have put those figures on the record because I think it is important to understand that in 1979 the amount paid by farmers on their debts for land and equipment equalled 36.1 per cent of their net real income, but by 1980 this had risen to 42.9 per cent, that is, the interest on the debts. Therefore, I well appreciate that Canadian farmers are facing serious problems in trying to plan their future purchases, as reflected in the downturn in the sale of agricultural machinery and implements.
The Canadian market is a substantial one. The 1981 market for farm machinery in current dollars is anticipated to be $2,068 million, which is a substantial sum of money. The Canadian demand in terms of North American production of farm machinery is 15 per cent, but Canadian production of North American farm machinery is only 9 per cent of the total North American production.
I suggest to the minister that we desperately need his voice in the efforts being made to resolve this dilemma. I do not deny for a moment that the farm machinery and implement industry-Massey-Ferguson in particular-is its own worst enemy. One of the primary reasons for the current position of Massey-Ferguson is poor management. It was not well-managed in the seventies. I think even its management today

December 10, 1980
Supply
will admit that that is true. However, certainly it would be to the detriment of Canadian farmers if we allowed that industry to disappear and fall by the wayside, because there is no doubt that the cost of imported farm machinery in Canada would be substantially increased if we were not manufacturing at all. While one might want to turn to Massey-Ferguson and say, "It is your own damn fault", the truth is that not only would the people employed in that industry suffer, but farmers across the country would suffer in the long run with no industry producing farm machinery in Canada for Canadian farmers.
Recognizing that poor management played a substantial role, we must also recognize that exorbitant interest rates faced by farmers, as well as by other people, are inhibiting when they attempt to plan purchases in coming years. It is also a severe inhibition to Massey-Ferguson to redevelop the company in a satisfactory and reasonable way.
Of course, what I said earlier about the decline in farm income is also an inhibition to planning for the orderly growth of the industry as it attempts to meet the needs of farmers. 1 think a farm machinery and implements industry is essential for Canada. There is no question in my mind that the contribution made by that industry to this country is substantial. 1 think the farmers of Canada need an industry here which can meet their needs. I believe farmers in Canada are concerned about what will happen, in terms not only of replacement of machines, but of replacement parts for the machines which they presently own. I am looking to this minister to accept that it is in our best interests as a country, and in the best interests of the farming community as a whole, to attempt to find a way to rationalize that industry, together with other similar industries, to try to come up with one rationalized, intelligent, competitive and supportable industry in Canada. 1 think it is also in the best interests of the economy of the country to attempt to do this.
1 would therefore ask the minister if he has given some thought to what, if anything, the government might be prepared to do to be of assistance. I ask the minister if he would be prepared to support at this time a task force made up of parliamentarians and also of people from the farming community and the industry itself to take a look at the farm machinery industry in Canada. They should take a look at how it operates, whether or not there is the need, which 1 suspect there is, to see whether there is a rationalizing process which can take place and whether or not there is a way in which we can fund a newly developed farm machinery and implements company in Canada which will be able to meet the need of the farmers, while at the same time meeting the needs of the workers who are presently faced with difficult times ahead.
I wonder if the minister could indicate whether he would be prepared, as Minister of Agriculture, together with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and anybody else who is interested, to establish this task force now. I ask the minister if he is prepared to make this task force representative of this House of Commons, representative of the farm community, of
the industry itself and of the financial community, and to set it a task. The task is to find a way to rationalize the industry in order that it will work in the interests of the farmer and of the Canadian economy, and to try to put together a package which will guarantee that we will not be paying exorbitant prices for imports in years to come for machinery which we could well have been, and ought to have been, manufacturing In Canada. Because of inadequate management over a number of years we have lost that manufacturing to foreign holdings.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a couple of things, and I notice you are pointing at me indicating that I have only two minutes.
With respect to the farm machinery industry, when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre corrected me the other day he was right; all duty on farm machinery was removed and there was free trade on farm machinery in 1944. That then started the dislocation of the farm machinery industry in Canada.
I was here for it.

The multinationals moved in and decided they were going to centralize production here and centralize production there. As a result, we do not have a really good farm machinery industry in Canada. My colleagues and I have had discussions, such as the one the hon. member has talked about, and we have had discussions with our counterparts in the United States to the effect that this industry must be divided properly and proportionately, at least in North America. I believe it should be better than the auto pact is. But it must be that kind of thing.
We can point to some parts of the Canadian farm machinery industry which are pretty healthy, such as Versatile Manufacturing in Winnipeg. The hon. member asks how we have helped the farm machinery industry. It may not have been in a magnanimous way but we helped Co-op Implements who were not out of the bushes economically. We loaned them nearly $9 million and arranged other co-op credit societies to become involved to keep them going. They are on an upward trend but they are not out of the bushes as far as economic problems are concerned.
I agree with the hon. member about the problems which Massey-Ferguson has. The other day I was talking to some people and I said I could have done as good a job as the president of Massey-Ferguson. I believe his salary is $272,000 a year. I said I could have done as good a job for $252,000 a year, and I do not think that would be an exaggeration.
I could have done it for nothing.

I am told that they did not even have a vice-president in charge of sales for Massey-Ferguson. Mr. Chairman, we do not sell farm machinery, farmers buy it. It is the same in the auto industry. The last Chrysler car I bought, I had to make an appointment to buy it.

Would you consider a task force?
December 10, 1980

Mr. Chairman, as this is the first time I have risen to speak in this chamber, I would like to take this opportunity to make hon. members aware of the area I represent. I am pleased to participate in these discussions concerning the budgetary estimates for the Department of Agriculture. I represent a constituency which is the county of Kent in the most southern part of Ontario, in fact, the most southern part of Canada.
Kent is the most productive county agriculturally in all of Canada. In fact, some of the highest quality farm produce grown in the world is harvested in Kent. In the year 1979 Kent county alone produced agricultural goods worth $227 million. Farmers in Kent have achieved the highest average yield per acre of all farmers in Canada in the growing of many crops, including corn.
At this time I will state a few statistics which I have here. We average 100 bushels of corn, soybeans 38 bushels, winter wheat 62 bushels-hon. members from the west will be interested in that figure-barley 63 bushels, and oats 84 bushels. We also grow tobacco and many vegetable crops, such as tomatoes, sweet corn and cucumbers, which are among the highest quality grown in Canada. Much of this achievement must be credited to the research and development which has been conducted by the federal Department of Agriculture.
Since the world's population is ever-increasing, foodstuffs will become more scarce and more valuable in the future, I have great difficulty understanding why the budget for the Department of Agriculture is only 1.3 per cent of the total federal budget. We must be willing to commit larger amounts of money, especially in the area of research, to fulfil our obligation to feed Canadians and the needy peoples of the world.
The agriculture industry employs the largest number of persons directly and indirectly compared with any other industrial sector in Canada. Agriculture should be receiving a much larger percentage of the federal budget.
Mr. Chairman, I would also like to make a few comments on the importance of transportation to the agricultural community. Agriculture is an industry which deals almost entirely with perishable products, which includes livestock in transit. Having travelled across Canada this autumn with the committee on transport, it was made apparent to me just how inadequate our transportation system is with regard to the movement of these perishable goods. Certain functions of the Department of Transport should come under the guidance of the Department of Agriculture. This should occur particularly in such areas as the shipping of potatoes, wheat, cattle, corn, soybeans and so on. No one knows better than the Department of Agriculture what types of cars are needed, whether they should be grain cars or refrigerator cars, the number of cars, what effect freight rates have on the price of the product and the amount of the subsidies. This would mean a great deal to the farmer when competing with producers from outside Canada, such as those of the United States.
Supply
I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture that the formulation and implementation of a Canadian agriculture export corporation has been long awaited by farmers throughout Canada. Many countries of the world would be interested in buying our farm products and taking advantage of our technical expertise in the agricultural industry if there were only salesmen out there promoting us. I am positive that we are missing many sales because of the absence of this type of corporation. We promised this assistance in the election campaign and the farmers are asking for it now. Since it would be in the best interests of the country, I believe we as a government should deliver on that promise.
The Minister of Agriculture is owed a debt of thanks for impressing upon the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the necessity and importance of classifying primary food production under the category A rating of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board. This is the highest priority rating for the supply of petroleum products in the event of an emergency.
While farmers generally accept the fact that fuel prices will increase, they are hoping that much time and effort is being put forward in the development of alternative energy sources. I can think of such fuels as gasohol, which can be used extensively throughout the farming community. Canadians are expecting much to be done in the research and development of alternative energy.
I would emphasize to the minister that a great hardship has been put upon farmers by the current high interest rates. Farmers in my area are faced with extremely high input costs and they have large mortgages due to the unrealistic price of farm land which has been caused by foreign investment. The price for land in my riding of Kent at the present time is in the area of $4,000 to $5,000 per acre. Anyone connected with the farm scene knows that present prices and revenues derived from agricultural products would barely pay the interest and there would be very little left to pay for fertilizer, seed, sprays, fuel, equipment repairs and equipment replacement. 1 feel that the federal government should initiate a short-term relief program to enable the farmer of Canada to survive this interest rate crunch. The story has been told of the farmer who, when asked after winning a $1 million lottery what he would do with this winnings, replied that he would continue farming until it was all gone. We must not let that happen.
1 think a few words of explanation are owed to the consumers of Canada. As was announced this week, food prices will be rising. I want to point out that the farmer should receive very little of the blame for those rising prices. Farmers receive a very small percentage of the market price for most of their products. It has been suggested that even if farmers gave away their wheat, the price of bread on our markets would not drop. As mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, Canadians continue to pay the lowest prices for food in the industrial world. These low prices would not be possible were it not for the efficient and effective agricultural practices employed by the Canadian farmer. I am sure that if the industry which handled our agricultural goods was equally

I would like to ask a question of the minister concerning the Farm Credit Corporation. He indicated yesterday, I believe, that changes were in the works in regard to the amount of money which may be allocated to the corporation. At present there are very few loans being approved. Speaking on behalf of the farmers in my area, many of whom have indicated to me that they have had to refinance, the amount of money available through the Farm Credit Corporation is inadequate. Would the minister comment, please?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kent and the hon. member for Hamilton West have mentioned the amount of interest which farmers must pay to borrow money. The Farm Credit Corporation's current rate of interest is 12.75 per cent. That is an enviable lending rate compared to what other people in society are paying. The highest rate of interest charged by the corporation was in the early part of the year when it was at 13 per cent. In 1979 the rate was 12 per cent and before that it was 10.75 per cent. It has been 10 per cent, and in 1959 it was 5 per cent. When one considers the earning ability and economics of agriculture, a 12.75 per cent interest rate in 1980, as compared to the interest rates that producers in other countries are paying, is not that bad.
1 cannot deny what the hon. member for Kent has said about the need for more money within the Farm Credit Corporation. There seems to be a need for unlimited funds in that corporation, and I wish we were in the position where we had unlimited funds. But when one looks at the amount of loans made by the Farm Credit Corporation to farmers in 1980, one will see that they total $358 million. In 1979 we made loans of $349,262,000. The amazing thing about this is that the loss in 1979 was so small that it could hardly be measured. The record of payment was excellent; .002 per cent. It will be about the same for 1980. Such an insignificant loss on the operation of the Farm Credit Corporation indicates a profit on the lending aspect of its operations.
I was amazed, Mr. Chairman, as were some others, to learn that as a Crown corporation the Farm Credit Corporation pays income tax on its profits. It is one of the few Crown corporations to do so when it finds itself in that position from time to time. Originally the Farm Credit Corporation was set up as a lender of last resort-the lender who would advance money to people when all other lending institutions had refused.
An hon. member referred to the difficulty young people have in borrowing money. If we think back to when the interest rate was 5 per cent and remember that the average wage at that time was about one-quarter what it is today, we can see that the present interest rate has not been a factor in inhibiting the efficiency of farm operations.
I repeat what I said earlier, that the number of young people entering agriculture today is not as insignificant as some would
have us believe. I hope that I will have more accurate figures available later this evening to show how many young people have entered agriculture in the last ten years. It is more than most people realize and I am happy to see it.
I know it is not as difficult to enter agriculture as it was when as a young man I tried to buy a farm. I did not have the advantage of the different types of programs that are available today, such as interest-free advance payments. The county of Kent and the county of Essex, where I live-it could be argued which county produces the highest quality food-together produce more food than some of the poorer provinces do, in dollar value. They have the heaviest concentration of agriculture of all kinds of nearly any spot in North America, except one place in California. When earning power was low it was difficult to pay even 5 per cent interest. Now that earning power is higher and interest is at 12.25 per cent, things are not as difficult with the help of the Farm Credit Corporation and interest-free advance payments, which mean that a commodity does not have to be sold when the market is low. It can be stored and sold when the market is right. The young farmer today is not faced with the disadvantage of distress selling.
The hon. member for Elgin, who is a former minister of agriculture, spoke about research. This is one of the reasons that Kent county is so productive. The hon. member mentioned that he had increased the budget for research but, Mr. Chairman, it is interesting to go over the figures and find when the biggest increase in the budget took place. There is not much difference but in 1976-77 $109 million was spent. I believe it was the hon. member for Lethbridge who said that $140 million was spent on research this year. Mr. Chairman, in 1979-80 $142.6 million was spent. The figure for 1980-81 is $155 million, an increase of $13 million. It was $117 million in 1977-78 and $133 million in 1978-79, which is the biggest increase for research in the past Five years. So I can claim fame as well as the former minister. 1 increased it more at one time and then he increased it at another time.
We believe that research is important, Mr. Chairman. It is important that we have more money available for it and it is also important that we have more money available for farm credit. We hope to introduce new legislation early in the new year which will give the Farm Credit Corporation the authority to go outside government as they see fit to raise funds when the need arises.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say initially that I think this is the first time in the eight years I have been in the House that the Department of Agriculture has appeared before this rather unique Committee of the Whole House. I am sure we appreciate the attendance of the minister for these two long days with his support staff, both on the floor of the House and in the gallery. I think it is most appropriate that they are here and we do appreciate it.
I am sure I will not surprise anyone in this House when I say I would like to put some comments on the record that deal with my favourite area of agriculture, the Canadian beef cattle industry. I want to confine my remarks to the current year
December 10, 1980

which is just winding down, 1980. These are personal remarks, Mr. Chairman.
Let me begin by saying that 1980 should have been a good market price year-I emphasize should-if only because of the position of our beef cattle cycle. Our breeding herd numbers- cows and replacement heifers-are only now barely beginning to increase. This phase of the cycle was expected to begin two or three years ago. That extension of the low part of the cycle must have caused all kinds of problems for the statisticians and people who make projections for any industry, especially the cattle industry.
Beef supplies in 1980 were not burdensome. In fact, they were down, at approximately 91 pounds per capita, at least 22 pounds per capita below the peak years of 1977-78. But 1980 was not a very good year for most cattlemen, both producing cattlemen and feeders. In fact, it was disappointing for five contributing reasons or factors.
First, and perhaps most important, we had an all-time record of supplies of competing pork and poultry. For the first time in our history, Canadian pork production exceeded, or will exceed, Canadian beef production. When that statistic came to my attention for the first time, I found it rather hard to believe. It is an indication of what supplies can do. For a while, live hog prices were as low on a per pound basis as one-half, and sometimes even less, of live fed steer prices. It is no wonder that pork consumption jumped and beef prices failed to respond to lower beef supplies as they traditionally do.
The second factor was the western agricultural drought. The minister has heard me comment on this many times both in this House and in committee, so I shall only say that it was very severe for the first six months of this year throughout most of western Canada. This followed the previous winter drought that produced none of the snow moisture that is so needed in western parts of this country in order to start spring growth and, in my own case, to start grass and begin the growth of hay crops. During April, May and June significant numbers of short yearlings, steers and heifers, had to move into feedlots. Normally they would not move until the fall of the year. Six months earlier than is the normal practice a lot of them had to be moved because of the drought situation. Even cows and calves were beginning to move to the market. That is most unusual in the early part of the growing season. There was no incentive whatever to hold back additional replacements.
When the rains finally came they were too late to make a hay crop. I am referring now to the traditional source of hay on cattle ranges that comes from flood schemes, small irrigation projects and so on. They had no moisture from snow to start the hay crop. There simply wasn't any; the rains came too late. In my own case, we put up about 5,000 bales, not the new big ones but the traditional small bales, when a year ago we put up about 45,000. That is an indication of what the half drought year did to us.

The third factor is interest rates, which have erupted twice this year. The first time they went from about 11 per cent to 18 per cent; that was last spring. Now they are back up to 15'/2 per cent. The realization is apparent, that they are still rising. It was these record high interest rates which caused cattle feeders to sustain their heaviest losses ever. No wonder they are gun-shy now.
Fourth, the beef cattle industry reflects the North American recession. I hate to say it, but I suggest we are still in it. We have high and rising unemployment, double-digit inflation and a very real slowdown in consumer incomes resulting in weakened consumer demand.
Fifth, we have steadily rising feed grain-especially barley-prices in Alberta and corn prices in central Canada. That, along with those interest rates, made the first half of 1980 a disaster cattle feeding period. Not only is that true in central Canada, but certainly in the west. They had a terrible half year in the feed lot operation. I doubt if they will completely recover by the end of this year.
Those five contributing factors have combined to shake our confidence as producers and feeders in our total cattle industry in 1980, and this is happening soon after that four-year price disaster of the mid-1970s in our cattle industry. In my opinion, the most visible and serious implication of the lack of cattle industry confidence is the two to three-year delay in the beginning of the breeding herd build-up across Canada. I refer now only to the beef cattle breeding herd.
Only last Friday in Calgary, at a one-day agricultural task force conference sponsored by the Canada West Foundation, when dealing with the ten-year outlook for Canadian agriculture in the 1980s, Jake Brown, the University of Saskatchewan dean of agriculture, a very highly regarded man, made the statement that it is highly unlikely that Canada will be able to move away from a net import base for beef by 1990 because of the lack of confidence in the future of our Canadian beef cattle industry.
The Minister of Agriculture was at that meeting. He must surely be aware of this lack of confidence. The minister was luncheon speaker at that meeting, but he probably did not hear Dean Brown's comments. I commend them to him. I hope he carefully examines the complete task force report or at least requires his staff to do so, as it is a fairly big report. It is very current and deals with the outlook for the decade we are now entering.
There are a number of other moves the minister might consider to restore that needed cattle industry confidence. For example, there is some unfinished policy direction respecting the federal drought policy. The minister will recall that the $67 million drought program covering herd maintenance and livestock fodder procurement was to benefit the western drought regions and, to quote an earlier statement about the drought, "parts of Alberta" would be eligible for these benefits.

It now seems that in Alberta only the Peace River district and an area around Camrose qualify for the herd maintenance program. Under the federal fodder procurement program, by definition most of Alberta will not be eligible. I regret that very much. I say to the minister, don't tell me that we in Alberta should not qualify because the rains finally came a little earlier than they did in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, which indeed they did, or because we have our wonderful irrigation system. As already indicated, in southern Alberta those welcome rains brought life and growth back to our grass, but I repeat, they never made a bale of hay.
Partly because of the subsidized hay costs, mostly for transportation, our choice irrigated alfalfa from Brooks and Taber and many other irrigation areas sold at $100 to $150 per ton before trucking charges were added. I am making the case for federal transportation assistance in Alberta, at least on a cost sharing basis with the Alberta government. 1 remind the minister there is between $5 million and $10 million of unspent and unallocated moneys in these two programs. I also remind the minister that his cabinet colleague, the minister of state responsible for the Wheat Board, said in Regina on August 8 that all moneys allocated for drought assistance would be spent on drought assistance. He said and I quote:
We're fully committed to pay the full amount. . . We will see what portion of the $60 million we have left and we will consult with livestock producers as to how we will pay out the balance.
The minister's new meat import bill should help stimulate some new confidence. I compliment the minister for bringing it in at this time. It is a program which we on this side have proposed for a number of years. We in the Conservative party have always supported the need for a beef import law in Canada. We chose to use that term. We fully support the countercyclical feature and the omission of live cattle, pork and canned meats.
I have some personal concerns about such things as some of the ministerial discretionary powers that are proposed, and with respect to the usefulness and make-up of the proposed advisory committee. However, I urge the minister to bring in the bill for second reading debate as quickly as possible. It is important that we have a good short second reading debate and get the bill into committee so that we can have the benefit of solid input from Canada's beef cattle industry.
There is one other most important and related item. I question the need for the GATT related requirement for the human population growth factor in the determination of meat import quotas. As I understand its operation, it is applied every year. The removal of this requirement would be a clear signal to our cattle producers that the minister does indeed care, and at least some long range incentive would be returned to us to get out and produce enough cattle and beef to be self-sufficient in Canada. We are not in that position now.
Further, this is the time of year for the annual calculations of our beef import quota levels for 1981. It is my understanding that the current year levels which were determined a year ago assumed a breeding cattle herd for 1980 that was too high since, as we know now, our breeding herd build-up has not
really begun, at least in significant numbers, as I indicated earlier in these remarks.
Will the minister make a correction for the 1980 formula level in calculating the 1981 quota levels? On this basis, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association indicated the new quota level would be in the neighbourhood of 146.6 million pounds. This level also agrees very closely with the traditional one-tenth relationship to the United States beef import level. One-tenth of their figure of 1.45 billion pounds comes to 145 million pounds.
However, the basic criteria that we should be following in Canada, and one which would be acceptable here, would make our protection equivalent to the offshore import protection of the United States. That is the important guideline. One-tenth of the American level would indeed do that and would be acceptable to our industry.
I have reviewed the Canadian beef cattle situation for the current year only and have cited evidence of and reasons for lack of confidence in both the short and the long-term outlook. I can assure the minister these are very serious concerns.
In closing, 1 submit most emphatically that our free market system for cattle in Canada is not a factor or part of the problem I have outlined, even though there may very well be some newer producers in the cattle industry who may feel that way. I want to remind the minister about my specific question concerning western drought and the portion of it dealing with the eligibility of parts of Alberta. His comments on that would be appreciated at this time.

Mr. Chairman, on the drought situation mentioned by the hon. member, we have made provision for the funds we said we were going to provide. The total funds we are going to provide for drought relief, I believe, are $67 million and this money will go to the people in need. At the present time, for the herd maintenance program there are 35,000 applications. What the hon. member is asking is if we would consider transportation costs in the province of Alberta. One of the predicaments we ran into on that is that when we first talked of drought assistance, the minister of agriculture for the province of Alberta said they had no drought and needed no assistance.
Not true.

1 am sure the hon. member remembers that later he said we did not provide any assistance for Alberta. I told the hon. member they have the right to appeal on any of these programs we have. The appeal board is being set up at the present time but how quickly it will get into operation, I do not know. We are setting up an appeal board with representatives from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and northern Ontario. The herd maintenance program is administered by another ministry, not by mine.
The transportation cost of fodder in Manitoba was not nearly as high. At one point we had allocated $1.6 million for
December 10, 1980

Manitoba. The accumulated amount of money spent to date is only $368,766. For transportation of fodder into Saskatchewan we had allocated over $1 million, and it has now cost $435,163. In northern Ontario the allocation was $400,000 and they did not use anywhere near the amount of money for the transportation of fodder.
The hon. member referred to the beef import law. I do not pretend that that law is the answer to all the beef producers' problems. He mentioned earlier the price of beef and the price of hay. That was a free market system probably working at its worst and not its best. It made some operations uneconomical and they were in a position where they had to purchase barley and hay at exorbitant rates.
It's the weather.

There was not a great dispersal of cattle according to our figures. I do not have the total figures past the end of September, 1979. There has not been the dispersal of cattle that people said there was going to be on account of the drought. Because of the programs we initiated we did instil some confidence in them. The hon. member answered his own question when he talked about the low price of beef because of overproduction of pork. Pork was sold at distressed prices and depressed the price of beef. Again, that is a free market system which is ill-managed, ill-supplied to the market and sold on the market at distressed prices. Beef did not resume a position where it would get a price which would afford a proper economic return to the beef producers. So we had high stocks of poultry, high stocks of pork and reasonable stocks of beef in Canada.

If I may, Mr. Chairman, I would like to share my time with my colleague from Roberval. Since coming here I realize that my Abitibi constituents are interested in a number of areas. We have seen that energy resources like electricity, wood residues, mines and the tourist trade are part of everyday life in Abitibi. Obviously, farming has been from the outset its raison d'etre, and still is a very active industry. We have farmers in the beef industry, in the chicken industry, and in the dairy industry, producing either whole or industrial milk. Quotas for natural milk are regulated by the Regie des marches agricoles, which means they are under Quebec jurisdiction. The milk goes to the pasteurizing plant and is thereafter consumed without further processing. The price is set by the Regie. Production is regulated to avoid possible overproduction that would drive prices below production cost.
I will not say anything further about whole milk, it being as I said under the Regie des marches agricoles, to supply the province's domestic market. I would like, however, to deal with a matter of interest to this House, which is the production of industrial milk under the Canadian Dairy Commission. Mr. Chairman, in Abitibi, in Quebec, our cows produce two types of milk. I understand they are now changing not the cows, but the system under which some cows produce whole milk, a
Supply
provincial type of milk, and others produce industrial milk that is under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Dairy Commission.
Some farmers, Mr. Chairman, have versatile cows. One day they give provincial milk and the next they give federal milk, when they have enough. I cheer up, Mr. Chairman, because I think they will soon be integrated. Mr. Chairman, I insist and say once again that the Canadian Dairy Commission system has proved to be essential for the stabilization of producers in Abitibi. Before 1963, the dairy industry was in pitiful condition. Following the suggestion of the dairy industry, the government set up the Canadian Dairy Commission which has been operating since then and is a vital instrument for the co-ordination of the dairy industry in Canada.
In July, 1980, Mr. Chairman, you stated the concern of the government about the allocation of quotas in some areas of the country. I know that several producers feel that their milk quota is an integral part of their heritage. It is normal that the milk producer should see in the allocation of quotas the only way to sell his product and he gives it a commercial value. We should not forget that to have obtained the assurance of selling his product is solely the result of a good and healthy national dairy policy. This is the first question which 1 would like to put to the minister: Following his press release of July 1980, could the minister specify his concerns about the fluctuations of those quotas?

Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Dairy Commission sets a national quota with the market supply management committee. They set a national quota, and that is distributed to the provinces. How it is distributed in the provinces is up to each separate and individual province.
The hon. member says the quota is a valuable thing and that some farmers feel it is their heritage. That is right, but very few provinces have the same system for pricing valuations on quotas. Industrial products are distributed freely across Canada and marketed freely across Canada, and then they are marketed on the world markets by the Canadian Dairy Commission. Some provinces have one class of milk. The hon. member said there are two kinds of milk. I was glad he clarified that. He said there is federal milk and provincial milk. In the province of Quebec there is probably more of a distinction between producers in one class and the other, although it is intended that they be put into one class. We say they should all be first-class Canadian high quality dairy producers because we now have better quality milk produced in Canada than we have ever had.
All I can say about the quota value is that I am concerned- whether it be for dairy or whatever-that there must be better control. However, we at the federal level do not have the authority to say what the quota should be for a producer within a province. We can recommend and suggest, as we have done, to the dairy farmers of Canada from time to time.

I do not know what more I can say at this time. As I said, the provinces do not have this, but when we look at quotas within the commercial industrial society, we see the same thing with respect to a taxi licence. If one tries to establish himself in the taxi business in the city of Ottawa, he will have to pay a very high price just to get a licence. There would be a quota to have one taxi. We have to be fair to producers who have bought quotas also. However, I have told the Canadian Dairy Commission to ensure that quota values are examined very closely. The chairman of the Canadian Dairy Commission himself has made two or three representations about which I know, to the dairy farmers of Canada to try to make sure that these quotas are kept at a realistic level or, if they are above a realistic level, that they return to a realistic level. Somehow they must be managed so that too few people do not get control of them. When young farmers want to get into the dairy industry when other farmers sell out, quotas should revert to the provincial milk marketing boards, as is the case in some provinces. It is then reallocated at reasonable rates to young people entering the dairy industry, or to anyone entering the dairy industry.

Mr. Chairman, at the convention of the dairy industry held on October 20, 1980, the chairman of the Canadian Dairy Commission estimated that the value of quotas would push the price of dairy products up by 10 to 15 per cent thus making them no longer competitive on export markets. The producers of the province agree with the present marketing policy. The chairman of the Canadian Dairy Commission suggested in his speech that unless the provinces implemented a new policy he would make it a point to recommend a different policy under which the value of quotas, as applied now, could no longer exist.
The minister assured the House this afternoon that the Government of Canada is willing to renew the stabilization program including a subsidy. Is the minister willing to increase that subsidy of $6.04 in 1975, seeing it is now really worth only $3.46, in 1980?

Mr. Chairman, we have no intention of increasing the subsidy because the subsidy for dairy farmers has stayed constant. Under the pricing formula we use, money comes from the marketplace, and that is the place from which it is intended to come. I would like to be out of the subsidy business. There is no doubt about that. We were removing subsidies from the dairy industry several years ago until the world price of industrial products collapsed. We then had to move in and save the dairy industry by renewing subsidies. At one time the subsidy was down to $111 million for industrial milk producers in Canada. We took the stand at that time that we must receive the return for dairy products from the marketplace. Many people do not understand that there is no subsidy for the whole milk we drink, but there are subsidies for industrial milk producers who have to compete in world markets. Our subsidies are not high when compared with subsidies in other dairy-producing countries, and I refer especially to European countries.
1 am well statisfied with the Canadian dairy policy. Our producers are about the best off in the world. I am sure our producers would like to keep the program the way it is since the formula price makes adjustments for changes in costs and for changes in the cost of living. Industrial milk producers know they are being fairly treated. I do not think it is necessary to index the subsidy, as some have suggested, as long as we have formula pricing. As 1 said earlier to another hon. member, I approve of formula pricing. This is the kind of system we have in many other parts of our society. If it is good for other parts of society, I do not see why it cannot work for dairy farmers.

Mr. Chairman, as member of Parliament for the riding of Roberval, I accepted the responsibility of representing and serving the whole population of that riding which is located north of Lac-Saint-Jean, an area that also bears that name. The main industries in the riding of Roberval are primarily those which depend on our wonderful natural resources, our forests. Indeed, three pulp and paper mills and several sawmills belonging to companies of international repute are located there of which, Domtar at Dolbeau and Mistassini, and Donahue at Saint-Felicien. Also, in Desbi-ens, there is a Saint-Raymond Paper plant which is currently experiencing production and profitability problems. The second industry in Roberval is agriculture. I will therefore take the opportunity today to deal with a matter which is close to my heart.
All Canadian farmers are faced with the same problems and difficulties. My constituents are no exception. I suggest that most farmers would be even less successful were it not for the help, the encouragement and the knowledge of their wives. I am neither a farmer nor a farmer's wife, but I have had the opportunity, within many organizations, to meet people from rural communities, and 1 want here to pay a special tribute to the farmers' wives who are perfectly able to operate their own farm or that of an ailing or deceased husband.
According to a study conducted two years ago by the Canadian Council of Rural Development, a woman spends an average of 29 hours working in the fields and in the farm buildings, keeping books and doing odd jobs, in addition to the 53 hours she spends on housekeeping duties. She is working, therefore, the number of hours required for holding two fulltime jobs, and for that, most of the time, she never gets paid. Because of the increasing number of men who are working full time or part time away from home, many women must replace them on the farm. Moreover, some of them, albeit a few, operate their own farms. Yet, the contribution of women to agriculture in Canada is not properly recognized.
December 10, 1980

As the Minister of Agriculture so eloquently stated before a large group of farmers' wives gathered for a convention here in Ottawa last week, and I quote:
I must recognize that men have not always been willing to give women a more visible place in agriculture. Also, we have not exactly encouraged women to seek management positions in national organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the Agricultural Union. It is high time the situation changed. Your participation in this convention is indicative of the fact that women want to be recognized as equal partners and have an input in the decision-making process, as they have the right to.
Mr. Chairman, I agree with the minister's statement and I should also like to remind the House that the AFEAS movement in Quebec has had a great part to play in the case which was brought before the provincial and the federal governments, namely, that of the right of women to a fair salary as partners with their spouses in the family business or farm.
I should now like to give a few statistics on milk producers in the western part of Lac-Saint-Jean. In my riding, there are 113 dairy farmers. Between August 1, 1979 and July 31, 1980, there were 21,937,476 litres of milk produced, 37.59 per cent of which was category 1 milk and the rest going to cheese factories. Mr. Chairman, when we speak of cheese in my area, we automatically think of Perron, from Saint-Prime, because this has been a family tradition for a hundred years now. As a matter of fact, the dairy industry started around 1880 in Saint-Prime, in the constituency of Roberval. At the beginning, they only made butter but in the last few years they added cheese making. That cheese factory received milk only four or five months a year. Then, cheddar cheese began to be exported to Quebec.
In those small plants there was no power supply and no electric lighting. Everything was made by hand. That industry developed slowly until 1955. Then because of centralization,
110 small plants had to close down in the area. Everything was centralized in Chambord for butter, cheese and milk powder. However, in 1963, Mr. Albert Perron, the present owner of the Saint-Prime cheese factory bought his father's plant dating back to 1895. In 1968, the plant was completely rebuilt, and in 1980 production reached the astonishing level of 15 million pounds of processed milk a year, which makes, 1.5 million pounds of cheese. I want to emphasize the fact that the Albert Perron Company Inc, won in 1970 the first world prize for cheddar cheese at the Royal International Dairy Show in London, England. In 1976 and in 1979, it won the Lys d'Or in Montreal and in Quebec City.
Mr. Chairman, I have given the historical background of that industry in my constituency because 1 sincerely believe that its administrators are serious and that they deserve support. Each year the plant faces a serious problem, namely, a short supply of milk, and consequently it cannot meet the demand of its customers.
Mr. Chairman, I would like some information on this subject. Is it because of poor milk quota distribution, and has the government considered developing an incentive program to

I am aware that the Canadian government provides assistance programs for these producers, and I shall come back to this matter on another occasion. 1 would like to congratulate the minister on the recent appointment of three women to senior positions on the Farm Credit Corporation advisory committee.
Hear, hear!

1 would like to add very briefly, Mr. Chairman, that these women will prove worthy of their appointment because of their ability and their qualifications and will contribute to the improvement of the quality of life in Canadian rural communities. I had two questions I wanted to ask the minister, but he has already answered them. First of all, as far as the subsidy is concerned-

Mr. Chairman, I have a series of questions for the minister, the first one of which has to do with the capital gains tax, a subject which was touched upon by my colleague, the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills. He spoke about the capital gains tax in some detail and he explained some of the problems which farmers were encountering when faced with this tax.
I might say to the minister that the capital gains tax has done a great deal to inflate the value of farm lands in the prairies. It is not uncommon for an elderly farmer to come into my office and ask me what it will cost him in capital gains tax if he disposes of his farm. He is usually very frank about it and tells me that what he will do is to add the amount of the capital gains tax to the selling price of the land. So not only do we have a situation where the ordinary inflation appreciates the value of farmland but we have, in addition, the capital gains tax which adds still further to the cost. In many cases this is quite a substantial amount per acre.
I recall that in the election campaign earlier this year a news conference was held in the city of Regina by the Liberal party, with a great deal of fanfare. It was indicated at the news conference that, if the Liberals were elected, they would be prepared to change the valuation day from 1972 to December 31, 1974. Every Liberal party candidate in western Canada went from meeting to meeting advertising the fact that this promise would be carried out if they were elected. Of course the promise was never carried out.

They will have fewer people believing them because of broken promises. Recently the provincial Liberal party indicated that as long as farmland remains farmland, no capital gains tax should be levied on the sale of that land.
Bearing in mind the promise made in the last campaign, could the minister tell me what is his party's position at the present time with respect to capital gains? What is the minister's personal opinion? What steps is he taking to see to it that farmers will gain relief from this oppressive tax?
