The hon. member can be assured that I will make those kinds of representations.

1 hope the minister will take steps at the next meeting of cabinet to impress upon his colleagues the importance of dealing with this subject.
Turning to the subject of the western grain stabilization plan, I believe the minister is jointly responsible for it. In the debates when the plan was proposed, when it went through committee stage and passed Parliament, I recall that the then minister who was putting the bill through indicated that it was the intention of the government to set up the plan in such a manner so that payments under the plan would be made in the spring of the year in order that farmers would have money available to start their seeding and spring work. As each year goes by, the decision on when a payment should be made under this plan becomes later and later in the year. For example, this year no decision was made until some time in November.
I realize the plan makes use of Statistics Canada to determine whether or not there will be a pay-out, and that the cost to the plan of Statistics Canada gathering this information runs at some $1 million. In committee a proposal was put to the government whereby the computer of the income tax department could be used to gather the information and to determine very quicky-perhaps within a month or so after the returns were filed-whether a payment should be made.
In view of the fact that each year the decision as to whether or not a payment is made becomes later and later, is there any intention on the part of the government to review the procedure by which information is gathered in order to determine what are the facts for the pay-out?

All I can say is that we want to be as efficient as we possibly can. It is an embarrassment to the ministers concerned with the program that we are not in a position to say, within one month of the year end of the grain marketing season, that we are able to make a decision. We had hoped that it would be swifter, but it does not appear to be. I cannot answer the hon. member other than by saying that we will continue to try to ensure that it is swifter, because a continual delay is not to our advantage; it is a political embarrassment.

Certainly it is not to the advantage of producers not to know or not to get paid until some time in the fall. If the minister is concerned, certainly he must be taking some steps to determine the reason for the delay in gathering the statistics used to determine whether or not there is a pay-out. Would the minister ask some members of his staff to read the minutes of the Standing Committee on Agriculture when the bill was before it and to consider our proposal which was placed before the then minister, Mr. Otto Lang, to see whether or not it could be used to speed up the procedure with respect to the western grain stabilization plan? Will the minister undertake to do that?
I will be meeting the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board tomorrow, and I will discuss it with him at that time.

Turning to another subject, yesterday the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster questioned the minister with respect to the sale of 30,000 tonnes of barley in the east earlier this year. I have read the comments of the minister as reported in Hansard of yesterday's date. A short time ago one of the commissioners of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Forrest Hetland, was reported in a publication entitled "Land" as saying:
"Look, we're shipping western barley into Ontario and Quebec to keep that market supplied, and we don't want their growers shipping barley out to the stronger markets." The board saw that starting to happen early in the summer but doesn't have direct control over marketing outside the prairies. It does, however, have authority to grant export and import permits for all Canadian barley, and it simply refused to grant any until domestic supplies were assured.
Then of course cabinet overruled the Canadian Wheat Board and the minister said yesterday that he was not in Canada at the time. He was out of the country, so he was not party to the discussions which took place. As reported in yesterday's edition of Hansard, the minister said:
-because I do not know, and I cannot find out what the traders were able to accumulate as a profit. I am told if a profit was made it was not passed on to any of the producers.
Then he went on further to say:
If the traders made an unwarranted mark-up on it, this is the kind of thing that makes one angry.
Could the minister tell the House to whom the special permits were granted for the export of this barley? If they were given to traders or grain companies, it would seem to me that the reason for doing that was because they had an oversupply of barley in stock; they did not want to lose money; and they prevailed upon cabinet to allow them to recoup some
December 10, 1980

of their loss. If this is what happened, in effect it was a subsidy by the producers of western Canada. To whom were these permits given, and for how much?

Mr. Chairman, normal sales take place and even under the embargo normal sales took place. If you will check there has always been, for at least the last five years, normal sales of Ontario barley outside of Canada. They asked for a permit for 30,000 tonnes. They accumulated approximately 15,000 tonnes, which was just shipped out in the last week to ten days. We have no way of knowing at what price.
I know one of the companies was Cargill and I am waiting for the name of the other companies. You quoted Mr. Hetland of the Canadian Wheat Board as saying that they shipped and they must supply grain to that market. I want to make it clear that the Canadian Wheat Board has supplied no barley to eastern Canada since April. The barley which was shipped to eastern Canada came from off-board barley. There was no onboard barley shipped down east at that time. This is a matter which is of concern to us and to the barley producers in Ontario. It is of concern to the barley producers all across Canada. But we must look at the insignificant amount that it was compared with total barley production and barley sales. Mr. Hetland was right when he said that we must look after them because the biggest consumers of feed barley are Canadians-80 per cent of all feed grains are consumed in Canada. They are the biggest customers and the ones which must be looked after.
We know that long-term barley sales have been made. I am sure the hon. member knows that the long-term barley sales which have been made were not that high priced, but the Wheat Board and the people who made these long-term sales would have been condemned if they were not doing that type of thing. They could not foresee that there was to be a drought and poor crops in China and Russia. These conditions were putting unwarranted kinds of pressure on top of the marketing ability, for the supply of that product. This put a tremendous burden on the over-all program for barley. Mr. Hetland was right when he said that you must supply that market because it is your best and biggest customer. The other people in the world may move in and out of the market as it warrants.
Mr. Chairman, I am coming back to long-term sales because they will show that they have been sold at lower than current prices. The pooling will show there will not be a big final payment on barley because those sales were made over a long-term period, something in the order of three years, when barley and corn prices were not as high as they are now.
I want to say that hon. members made no comments about what I said yesterday about making those same kind of long-term deals with the Canadian Livestock Feed Board makes. They will not only serve what you call eastern Canada, but one of the biggest users of that grain is British Columbia, which depends on that kind of grain. We are not just talking about people in the eastern part of Canada, we are talking

about people in the western part of Canada who depend upon that grain also under that same pricing.
Let us be fair. If it is to be good for somebody in the Middle East or in Europe to buy barley under those conditions then it should be good for the biggest consumer of all feed grain produced in Canada, the Canadian livestock and poultry producer. Let him or her have that same kind of agreement and that same kind of contract.

I would just like to say that the minister has indicated that one of the shippers was Cargill, and I assume that there may have been one or two other companies which obtained permits to ship. It would seem to me that, therefore, it was not the producers in Ontario who were making the money but it was the grain companies. In other words, Cargill and the other grain companies had a surplus of grain in Ontario. The price, undoubtedly, would drop because of the surplus they did not want to sell at a lower price, so cabinet went over and above the Wheat Board and allowed Cargill and others to sell it on the world market at the expense of the western grain producer. I ask the minister if that is not a fact.

Mr. Chairman, I would say it is at the expense of the Ontario barley producer, who always receives less for his barley than the western barley producer; it is always $20 to $30 a tonne less than western barley, in Ontario. So if there was a mark-up, and we do not know that for sure, it is estimated it could have been anywhere from $40 to $45 a tonne. It was a conglomerate of grain companies. There were four I am sure: Cargill, Richardson, Continental, and Northern Sales.
I can say that the representation was made to me, not by any of those grain companies, but by the provincial ministry of agriculture in Ontario on behalf of their barley producers. Not one grain company made representation to me and I know of no grain company making any representation to anybody else. They may have been the ones which made that kind of profit. As I said yesterday, that is a very bad thing because producers would not make that kind of profit in two, three or four years of production. They would not make that kind of profit per tonne.
The marketing system we operate under seems to be the one which the hon. member's party condones, that is, a free market system working at its very best. If you do not want that system, tell us then that you abhor it and that you want us to put everything under the Canadian Wheat Board. That is what the Canada West Foundation said the other day. They said, "Have it all under the Canadian Wheat Board, or all on the free market system." Maybe that is what we should be doing. It seems to me no matter how fair you try to make this system work it just seems to add more confusion to it. They are complaining about what the Russians may have made under a long-term contract-maybe it was 100 per cent they were making profits on-but nobody seems to say that about the foreign buyer. They are talking about what has happened right within our own country and I come back, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that those people of ours who are feeding their stock

That was quite interesting, Mr. Minister, but the fact remains that there was a profit made and it appears that it did not go into the hands of the producer.
One short question. The minister is aware of the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund which has some $9,066,000 on hand, which is producers' money. Fie is aware of the need for research. He has been given the means of using this money for research and I am wondering what his position is, because every day that goes by the producer is losing $3,500 in interest.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows I agree in principle with what he wants to do. I said so before I went on my sabbatical, when I was minister before the short sabbatical I took. Well, I have not changed my mind on that. I think that money should be for the benefit of western farmers, for western research. Lord only knows, the hon. member knows as well as I, that we could use that $9 million so well. We have a bit of a dispute as to whether we should just turn it over into a fund with a committee to administer it, etc. But we are ready to move on that very quickly. Whether we can make a proper agreement with the hon. member or whether he can accept my bill when it comes to the House is something we will have to see, but we will work for the good of the farmers on this, I know.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that the words of the minister of late are very interesting. I suspect that a number of us on this side of the House have become strong advocates of the sabbatical system and would certainly encourage him to continue with it.
The particular topic before us tonight has provided one of the most interesting debates I have read in Hansard and sat in on for a long time. It is a topic which touches all of us very closely. Indeed, it touches citizens right around the world whether they be young or old, rich or poor, living in eastern or western Canada or in any other part of the world. I suspect that people are very concerned as never before as to what the future holds with regard to the current trends in agriculture, food production, and the direction of the entire food industry.
Many people are wondering about Canada's role in this industry. One hears a great deal about petropower and nuclear power and the whole concept of agripower. The whole area will be of greater interest to us as Canada plays a greater role in feeding the world population.
Over the years Canada has been proud of its accomplishments in the area of research and development. Indeed, scientific inquiry originating in Canada has led the way in many
areas. Many Canadian inventors and scientists are known around the world for their accomplishments in the world agricultural community. Yet the budgeted funds for research and development in agriculture are less today than in the past. It is important that Canada keep up in this ever-changing field where many people around the world are experimenting in such areas as new strains of grains, new types of beef production and new ways of growing vegetables. It is important that the government make a commitment to research and development, not for two years or five years, but for 25 years. Only then can we tell the scientific community that the commitment is there and young people can train in our institutions to participate in this research in the future.
My question to the parliamentary secretary is this. Is the Department of Agriculture prepared to make a commitment to more scientific research in the field than exists today? Is the government prepared to stand up and say, "Yes, this is in the best interests of Canada and its agricultural future so we will commit ourselves to increasing the budget for scientific research in agriculture?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in reply to the question of the hon. member opposite about the research programs, I would like to tell him that whatever the programs put forward by the Canadian government, the Department of Agriculture will definitely have its share, as we have seen this year, since the $140 million budget was increased to $150 million. In the future, research programs, and I am referring to all government departments, Agriculture Canada will definitely have its share.

Mr. Chairman, when one considers the cost of scientific equipment and of inflation, the government has added very little if anything to the budgets of past years, and even what it has added is recognized by all people in the agricultural sector as inadequate. I mean that as a positive criticism and I hope that the parliamentary secretary and the minister will give real consideration to increasing the funds to this most crucial area. The same case could probably be made for a number of other areas.
Strong leadership from the minister is required. As in the many sectors of the government, there is a lack of leadership. In agriculture we have seen the disappearance of first class land and growing monopolistic control over food production and distribution. In a sense it will mean the growing dependence of Canadians on foreign producers as we become more and more dependent on foreign suppliers in the food sector. We lack a buy-Canada policy and a grow-Canada policy. Is the parliamentary secretary able to stand up and say, "Yes, my department is prepared to take a strong position and make a commitment to encourage a buy-Canada policy and a grow-Canada policy in a rigorous way."?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, first, as far as the funds for research are concerned, I would say to the hon. member that 20 per cent of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are earmarked for research. As the minister explained it on several occasions this afternoon, it is the highest percentage of all funds spent throughout the world on agricultural research and I think that Agriculture Canada and all Canadians should be proud of such achievement.
With respect to land conservation, I would say to the hon. member that under the Canadian Constitution, the conservation of farm or arable land is entirely under provincial jurisdiction.
As for his third question, the department is very conscious of the problem raised by the hon. member and, as Agriculture Canada has always done in the past, we are trying by all possible means to provide better conditions to Canadian farmers while protecting the consumer.

Mr. Chairman, we heard earlier about the fact that the number of farms in Canada is diminishing as a result of more sophisticated machinery. There is also the fact that more energy is being consumed. One can make the case that Canada is the most inefficient food-producing country in the world when it comes to energy. To gather one calorie of energy from food requires four calories of energy using our system, whereas in other systems one calorie of energy results in four calories of foodstuffs coming back. Are we sensitive enough to the role which energy plays in our "efficient food production system"?
I was intrigued by a recent study conducted in the city of Vancouver which says that with the amount of arable land available in that city two million persons could be provided for under an efficient system. Has the parliamentary secretary given much thought to the utilization of the techniques of urban farming as a way of minimizing the amount of energy required to produce foodstuffs for Canadians, and as a way of minimizing the amount of energy required for the transportation of foodstuffs from California, Florida, Mexico or wherever?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the hon. member that Agriculture Canada, of course, is well aware of the calorie-costs problems involved in producing foodstuffs, and we try to save energy in all areas of research, whether in the use of greenhouses, nitrates, plants and crops of all kinds. Agriculture Canada is using all possible means to limit energy and oil costs in the production of foodstuffs. Quite recently, a committee was established for the sole purpose of studying the energy problems Agriculture Canada will have to face within the next decade.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to have a few moments tonight to speak to the Minister of Agriculture on this subject, to lay down a few principles on the whole question of food and international hunger, and the responsibility of food producing countries like our own in relation to the starving people of the world.
I had hoped that the minister would remain in the House during my remarks, but I appreciate that he might be hungry himself at this time. He has gone to supper. I thought that in the context of his own hunger we could have spoken more directly about this human problem that faces something like 800 million people on the face of the globe today.
During the last six months I have had what I consider the privilege of being a member of the North-South Committee on International Development. That committee will be issuing its report next week, probably on Tuesday, when it will make some specific recommendations regarding food, to the minister and his department.
The reason we approach the whole question of food was because of a common knowledge that this is a major international problem. The Brandt commission report that was produced about a year ago stated:
This commission sees no more important task before the world community than the elimination of hunger and malnutrition in all countries.
On this whole question of hunger, I think it is important to realize that it is more than a lack of food. I have seen many cases where hunger not only produced the phenomenon of being hungry but also produced chronic diseases and illnesses, physical and mental retardation, as well as a lethargy which compounds the whole area of development and brings about non-productivity and early death.
Without a well-nourished population capable of working, a developing country will remain dependent on external forces for development, and a self-sustained and self-generated type of development will not be attained.
When we address the problem of hunger and the production of food, we are striking at one of the most profound problems underlying the whole area of underdevelopment. To put it simply-people starve to death because they cannot buy food. They do not have the economic base themselves to buy food. We rarely see a rich person dying from hunger. Although that sounds a too simple explanation, nevertheless when situations arise in which populations cannot receive enough for their labour, or whatever, to buy food, there is the problem of starvation.
I think it is extremely important that as we consider the whole question of international hunger and the production of international food, we be aware that the women of the planet produce the most food; that the women of the planet care for and look after food.
Many times when we get into discussions with the Department of Agriculture relating to quotas, wheat sales and so on,

December 10, 1980
Supply
we forget that, in most of the world, food production, care and preparation are in the hands of women. The solutions which lead to the elimination of starvation, it should be remembered, will probably come from women. This is a simple fact that is often forgotten when we talk about agribusiness and big farming. We forget that women using hoes are growing most of the world's food.
Many of the myths related to food have to be considered at this time as well. Some presentations made to the North-South Committee whose report will be ready for public scrutiny soon, contain matters of importance. People have traditionally been led to believe that hunger was the result of overpopulation, insufficient food production, or adverse soil and climatic conditions. The FAO and other international organizations such as the World Bank, the Commonwealth group of nations and so on, seriously question this simple explanation of that world problem.
We know that even in Bangladesh, one of the most densely populated countries in the world, enough grain is produced to provide a minimal diet for all its people. That follows a time of mass hunger. The FAO has also indicated that the earth as a whole produced enough grain to provide each of us with adequate protein and more than 3,000 calories per day, exclusive of all the fruits, vegetables and grass fed meats that are produced.
When we think about the fact that we have this technology and the resources and the possibility to feed all the world's people, we realize that it is a sin that 800 million people are starving.
Something is lacking, Mr. Chairman. Many things are lacking. One is the political will in many of the developing countries to see food as one of the primary necessities and to consider that the production of food must become one of the first political principles.
The report I have mentioned will discuss food aid, distinguishing very carefully between emergency food aid in situations where there is no other solution except aid or long-term aid, not in the form of food as such, but in a form which will enable people to produce their own food.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary about the philosophy or policy of the Department of Agriculture at this time, regarding the whole question of food aid.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In reply to our colleague opposite, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), in co-operation with the international organization FAO, has a very important role to play in developing agriculture. Canadians are indeed privileged in that they have land, technology and human resources to continue developing agriculture. We are already doing quite a lot to feed the hungry of the world, but we hope to do a lot more to feed them by the year 2000. Of course, also for the benefit of the Canadian economy, as I mentioned in my remarks yesterday, Canadian farmers should increase their productive capacity.
As I said a moment ago, Canadians are really privileged. We are aware that because of the high quality of our soil and farmers, we can do more for developing countries. The eighties will certainly be the decade of agriculture and food throughout the world. As I often say, the seventies have been the decade of energy. The eighties will be the decade of agriculture and food. To conclude, I should like to advise the hon. member that steps have already been taken to celebrate October 16 of next year as International Food Day, and that the Minister of Agriculture will actively participate in the ceremonies to help developing countries.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a few questions to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture.
Before doing so, however, 1 should like to start with a preamble on the evolution of agriculture in Quebec and in Canada generally. Speaking of agriculture, not to go too far back, around the years 1789-1840, the evolution at that time- that was the subject of my thesis for a Master's degree-was much the same as that we are witnessing today in that, in order to increase agricultural production and have surpluses, man was forced into revolutionizing agricultural methods and techniques, naturally. The same phenomenon occurred in French Canada and English Canada, under the aegis of a Liberal government which, I might say, proceeded with an agricultural revolution while we went about our industrial revolution.
I remember when I was young back home, 200 farmers produced about as much as five farmers today in our area. That, of course, we owe to more sophisticated techniques and to the improvement in our agricultural schools. One can say that agriculture in Canada is at this point in time the most evolved and advanced in the world. Today, I heard one of the speakers say that the average farmer in Quebec or Canada today can feed about 50 persons. Those statistics are about 20 years old. Today a farmer in French Canada can feed at least 100 to 125 persons; we may even be ahead of the Americans on that score. Therefore, I am not ashamed, I am proud to congratulate our agriculture ministers and our governments for the great work they have done in feeding the Canadian people and others. We are now selling wheat to the Chinese and the Polish. I must therefore-it is my duty as a Canadian- congratulate the people who devoted themselves, who perceived and saw the future of agriculture in Canada. Now, I should like to put a few questions to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture.
In my area, along the shores of Lake Saint-Pierre, this year the corn crop was bad and life is pretty rough. I am therefore wondering whether the Department of Agriculture will be able to make up for the losses and help the farmers.
December 10, 1980

In the future will the Farm Credit Corporation allow young farmers to borrow money, at reasonable rates of interest, which was pointed out earlier today, and spread out over many years? Otherwise, debts strangle them, and they cannot take over the farms; we know how much they cost. So, is the Minister of Agriculture now willing to help the young buy a farm and go into business for themselves?
My third question has to do with Canada geese. For the past 50 or even 75 years this problem of Canada geese has been lingering, yet these birds are still there and will continue to be there while causing damage to our agriculture especially in my riding because that is where they stop over every year in the fall and on their way back in the spring. Are the Government of Canada and the Department of Agriculture prepared to compensate, under agreement with the provincial government of course, the losses incurred by farmers because of damage caused by Canada geese? My fourth question deals with pesticides. Every year when the corn fields are blooming, insecticides and pesticides are sprayed over them, so as a result bees that feed on cornflowers die.
I kept bees myself at one time, and 1 know what I am talking about. Beekeepers now lose about half of their hives because of pesticides sprayed on corn. There are about 60,000 bees in a hive during the season they gather honey from flowers. So, about 30,000 bees in each hive die each and every year and consequently do not produce honey because of those pesticides sprayed on corn. What is the government or the department going to do to make up for the beekeepers' losses?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall answer our colleague from Richelieu. If my memory serves me right, he asked four very good questions. First of all, in the case of the corn program, we are aware, of course, that in some areas, crops were more or less good this year. However, there is a crop insurance program and there can be no support payments by the Agricultural Stabilization Board based on the current price of corn. When the board steps in, it does so on the basis on the last five years. Since the price of corn grain has been rather high over the last five years, it is not anticipated that support payments will be extended for the year 1980, which is almost over. The producers will have to-and I would like to tell the hon. member that this situation is not general throughout Quebec or throughout Canada, because in certain areas farmers were able to harvest well ahead of time and fairly easily; that may be saying much, but they were able to harvest.
As far as farm credit is concerned, in his second question the hon. member talked about finding ways and means to help young people enter agriculture. First of all, the farm credit interest rate has now been set back to 12.75 per cent, which is lower than the bank rate. I would also like to point out to the hon. member that 75 per cent of Farm Credit Corporation loans are made to persons under the age of 35. So I think it is not all that bad. Of course, it remains to be seen what
Supply
mechanism could be found to help young people aged 20 who do not have the necessary assets.
But on the whole I think that with all the services and facilities provided by the Farm Credit Corporation and other such agriculturally-oriented lending organizations the sons of farmers do manage to buy farms. As far as the goose program is concerned, the hon. member will recall that the minister, the deputy minister and myself met a few months ago with the people in his riding and we said at the time that they should go to the Quebec departments of agriculture and the environment. Afterwards, the department studied the matter, as usual, and published a press release indicating that it would help some western farmers whose crops had been damaged by migrating birds. 1 think the people we met at the time with the hon. member for Richelieu had built up a very solid case for themselves. I do not know if they presented their case to the Quebec departments of agriculture and the environment but if they did a study will be done by both levels of government, that is by the Quebec agriculture department and Agriculture Canada and the Quebec environment department and Environment Canada.
As for compensation for problems with bees this year, I will say this: farmers must use pesticides and herbicides. One is called Furoden. If it is sprayed from the air, it may cause damages. The label on the product warns against spraying it from the air. It must be applied at ground level. We will therefore have to establish how this herbicide or pesticide was applied and under what conditions. I think that pretty well answers the four questions put by the hon. member for Richelieu.

Mr. Chairman, there is no need for me to describe the geographical situation of my riding that rejoices in the name of Temiscamingue, the former stronghold of my famous predecessor, Mr. Real Caouette. It encompasses the Temiscamingue area proper and part of the Abitibi area. La Sarre, for example, is a town in my riding located in northwest Quebec, quite close to the 49th parallel.
Farming in northwest Quebec started in the twenties and some 30 years sooner than in the Temiscamingue area. The whole area was an outlet for social unrest and unemployment during the depression years. In those years, we succeeded in clearing some 550,000 acres by hand, by the strength of our arms and with determination, and I would add, Mr. Chairman, with oaths, and those 550,000 acres, for farming purposes only, cost the government and the farmers themselves huge amounts of money.
What has happened in the last few years, I would say since the early sixties? I understand that agriculture, as any other sector of the economy, has been transformed and undergone an inevitable and necessary metamorphosis. This compounded the

December 10, 1980

difficulties that plagued the farmers of my area in the sixties. Difficulties that are undoubtedly linked to artificial rains.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, many will be surprised to hear me today talk in the House about artificial rains. But it is the honest truth. I have the evidence, the names of the companies that made the tests and the amounts of the contracts that were awarded. Those tests have purely and simply ruined farming in my area. I well remember a ten-year period of continually foul weather and steady rain. And it lasted throughout the summer season. How many times 1 have seen farmers who had to wait for the first fall frost to retrieve their machinery from the fields and it pull out "by the neck", as we used to say, with a chain and a tractor and, of course, the crop was completely lost. It is the plain truth, Mr. Chairman. Once again, without us knowing it, of course they had chosen the Abitibi-Temis-camingue area to carry out experiments in artificial rain. As 1 said, this was the death sentence of agriculture in my area. From 550,000 acres of farmland, there was a dramatic drop to some 200,000 acres. Of 11,000 farmers in the Abitibi-Temis-camingue area, there are only 1,400 left today.
The effects of this sharp decline in the farm population are inevitably being felt by the population as a whole, that is, the total population is growing older as the young people leave the area. There is an alarming decrease in population. What are we to do in such a situation? There is not much hope of attracting big companies such as General Motors or Ford or any other. Of course, those people are not very interested in building a plant in Abitibi-Temiscamingue.
Now, if we want to go on living in our area, what can we do exactly? Naturally, several responsible organizations and individuals have looked into the problem. For my part, 1 met with regional officers of the Quebec department of agriculture, with FPU officers and its president, Mr. Boulet. All those organizations, all those people agree that we must develop a beef cattle industry. First, we are far from self-sufficient in Quebec in beef production. Secondly, at the Kapuskasing experimental farm, in Ontario, which is close to our area, they have developed crops that are most suitable to our area. As ensilage is increasingly used, it is now quite easy to harvest crops, or should I say, to save crops. The artificial rain experiments stopped a few years ago, and 1 can assure you that as long as 1 sit in this Parliament, they will not be resumed unless, of course, the people make a formal request, which I doubt very much.
Fourth, in the past producers have suffered from price and market fluctuations. One year prices were good, but they were down the next year and producers went bankrupt. That does not happen any more thanks to the stabilization program.
Fifth, as I said at the beginning of my speech, we have an enormous reserve of agricultural lands which sell at ridiculously low prices. One never hears about lands selling at $2,000 an acre as it happens in the southern part of the province around Saint-Hyacinthe, for instance, or in southern Ontario or in the
prairies. Back home land sells for a few hundred dollars an acre.
Since my time has expired, I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if I could urge the minister to have a study made in my region on this subject. If that study shows that it would be profitable to produce cattle, would the minister be prepared to help us through special programs?

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to discuss agriculture with the minister and his officials. The topic of agriculture is a very important one in my riding of Hastings-Frontenac, in Lennox and Addington and, indeed, across Canada. It has been recognized that one out of every four Canadians works in a field related to the food and agricultural industry. In 1979, farm cash receipts totalled some $14 billion. This figure is multiplied as the money taken in by farmers goes through the Canadian economy. There is no question that a healthy growing agricultural economy contributes greatly to a healthy, growing Canadian economy. With record unemployment and inflation in Canada today, the economy needs all the leadership it can get.
There is no question in my mind that the Canadian farmer has been the real strength of this country. It has been the farmers ability to lead by example, to thrive on challenge and to increase efficiency which has built Canada.
I would like to look at some of the areas in which the federal government has shirked its responsibilities to the agricultural industry. The recent budget put forward by the government virtually ignored agriculture. There was no mention of allowing farmers to roll over tax-free the proceeds of the sale of their farm lands into registered retirement savings plans. The budget introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West last December would have provided this worth-while measure. In the latest budget there was no mention of updating the V-Day values used to determine capital gains tax, as promised in the election campaign. These measures concerning capital gains are very important to farmers across this country. As a farmer's retirement income lies in his land, the selling price of a farm has to reflect these high potential capital gains, and as a result the high start-up costs are prohibitive to many who would otherwise be entering farming.
1 am happy to see that the present government has followed the lead of the Conservative budget of last December by allowing the deduction of income paid to a spouse in a non-incorporated business. This is good news for farmers who may now take advantage of this measure which, I understand, is to go into effect for the 1980 tax year. It also recognizes the hard work done by farm wives on farms.
The Canadian food system accounts for about 17 per cent of total energy use. Thus the agricultural sector will be hard hit by the government's misguided energy policy, which already appears to be creating more problems than it will solve. Energy self-sufficiency is already suffering.

There is no mention in the budget of exempting fuels used in food production from the federal excise tax, as the Crosbie budget proposed. There is no energy tax credit, as was proposed in the Crosbie budget, to help low and middle-income Canadians adjust to rising energy costs. How is the Canadian farmer expected to show leadership when the federal government shows little itself?
The Progressive Conservative government last year showed leadership in various provisions put forward in its budget and energy program. Several of the proposals in the Crosbie budget have been adopted by the present government, and I hope the minister and his government will also extend some relief to farmers to help them play their important role in the Canadian economy even better.
This past summer many farmers in Frontenac and Lennox and Addington counties supplied hay for the Manitoba emergency hay assistance transportation program. Under this program, Ontario hay was shipped interprovincially by rail to Manitoba farmers to help overcome difficulties associated with the drought conditions there last summer. 1 understand these rail shipments were subsidized by the railways and the federal and Manitoba governments. Many Ontario farmers were eager to help their Manitoba counterparts by supplying hay to dealers, who in turn shipped the hay west. As it turns out, many farmers in my riding have not yet been satisfactorily paid for the hay supplied. There appear to be conflicting stories about hay quality and weights and financial responsibility for these discrepancies. I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he is aware of the problems brought about by this emergency hay program and what action he and his officials might consider taking to correct shortcomings which are a serious matter of concern to farmers of both Manitoba and Ontario.
The federal government has managed to break another promise through its recent cancellation of funding for Can-farm. As hon. members may know, Canfarm had been run by Agriculture Canada in co-operation with the provinces and universities prior to a transfer to a consortium of farm organizations and co-operatives in March of 1979.
Canfarm is a computerized farm record keeping and financial planning service with offices across Canada. The programs administered by Canfarm are very useful and help Canadian farmers become more efficient and competitive through computer analyses of their business operations.
The government tried to eliminate Canfarm in 1978 in a series of cost-cutting measures. Later, after realizing the full importance of Canfarm, it did agree to consortium bridge financing and loan guarantees. Canfarm was promised a $4 million loan guarantee and grants of $1.2 million by the federal government during its first three years of operation to help in a smooth transition to the private sector.
The Progressive Conservative government was honouring those commitments, but the present government has recently reneged on its funding by cancelling further bridge financing to Canfarm . This is just one more way in which the present government has failed in its commitments to agriculture. 1

have received letters and telegrams from constituents and organizations reflecting their concern about the government's stopping its funding to Canfarm. I share the concern of these people, who have found Canfarm a vital service and who feel they would face great difficulties without it.
Since becoming privatized, Canfarm has been working hard to organize and design its services to meet the needs of farmers. Officials are working to build up the number of farmers using its various services. In Canfarm's annual report for 1979 President Peter Hannam in his "President's Message" stated, and I quote:
The stage has now been set to expand beyond the growing pains of 1979 and to take advantage of the opportunities in the 1980s.
He also noted that the founding members of Canfarm's co-operative services-some 14 farm organizations and cooperatives-have broken new ground in establishing Canada's first national farm management co-operative.
In light of the minister's decision to cut off further bridge financing to Canfarm it appears that the minister is closing the door to any opportunities in the eighties, and instead of soothing the growing pains of Canfarm, he is attempting to administer the death blow.
Any transition of a business or agency such as Canfarm requires time, support, hard work and money to make the transition work. The Canfarm program is designed to help the Canadian farmer. Farming, as 1 have mentioned, is a vital component of our economy.
We hear constantly of government programs to supply money, goods and services to other countries to help them develop various services. This is commendable, but it does not mean that services at home in Canada need to suffer as a result. By withholding the financing it requires the minister and his government are refusing to support Canfarm. The amount is trivial compared with the large sums the government spends. It is to help Canadian farmers in their effort to improve their industry, an industry on which Canada was built.
Amid announcements of Canadian aid in the millions of dollars for projects in other countries and the recent announcement of an additional spending of $17 million for self-serving propaganda advertising within Canada to further the government's misguided constitutional package, could the minister please explain why his government has announced its cancellation of financial aid to help Canfarm, a Canadian program which was helping Canadian farmers?
Why is the government so mixed up in its spending priorities, and why does it continue to forget and insult the farmers? Realizing the tremendous contribution agriculture has made to the development of this country, I find it hard to reconcile the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture with the positions taken by the federal government. The minister said:
We really should have a national farmer appreciation day. People become too complacent when it comes to the successes of agriculture. As long as you are efficient, productive and doing a good job, everyone seems to take everything for granted. Well, I for one won't, and I'm doing my best so that others won't either.

The cancellation of financing to aid Canfarm, the lack of relief for farmers from the rapidly rising energy costs, and the hidden costs of capital gains, are just some of the sorry indications of the lack of leadership shown by the federal government with respect to the farming industry. Mr. Chairman, Canadian farmers do not have to look too far to see who really takes them for granted.
The minister has referred to the heritage of the Canadian farmers as being the acceptance of responsibility, meeting challenge and defying hard work. The government should reward such a sector of our society by helping them provide an example to all Canadians, not by forgetting about them or taking them for granted just because they have overcome the government's indifference in the past.
We must look to the future, Mr. Chairman, and face the problems head on. The government could use its majority in a constructive way to unify Canada and provide a realistic energy package. We have already seen the results of the government's efforts to unify the country and create energy self-sufficiency.
Agriculture helped build this country with roots deep and strong, and these same roots will help preserve Canada. Determination, sharing and hard work have helped to overcome adversities in all shapes and forms. Tradition was strong. People were slow to change from the known to the unknown for the sake of change alone.
Canada is a large country with diverse geographic and climatic regions. Canadians in one region regularly receive adverse weather from another region, compliments of mother nature. Farmers in particular are hit the hardest by these natural phenomena. Life goes on as people learn to live with something over which they have little control. But when the force that slams the farmer and other Canadians is the federal government, that is a very unnatural phenomenon. People do have control since the government is accountable to the people for what it does. The lightning has gone out from Ottawa, and now the thunder is rolling back in.
So, in concluding my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture and his government not to forget the farmers of this country and not to take them for granted. It is for the government to follow many of the attributes accorded to the farmer; those of leadership, self-sufficiency, unity, efficiency and hard work, which will bring about solutions to the very real problems facing Canadians.
Instead of planting the seeds of discontent, the government must sow the seeds of unity. The government must try to understand all of the variables that make a country grow strong, just as a farmer nurtures a crop. The government must know when the crop is healthy before it tries to transplant it to uncultivated fields. Just as a farmer cannot set arbitrary dates for when it would be most convenient to harvest the crop, the federal government cannot set unrealistic deadlines affecting the future of our great country.
I can only hope that the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues in the months ahead do not lose further sight of the strong heritage and leadership shown by the agricultural industry in Canada and its importance in feeding Canadians as well as hungry people throughout the world.
Agriculture has provided the strong roots for the future. Farmers know that after a threshing there is a lot of chaff. Canadians will not be threshed by a government gone out of control. Our future will not be chaff thrown to the wind. Our roots are too deep.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member made a great representation about Canfarm, and rightly so, if he feels so strongly about it. Again I come back to the conference which took place here in Ottawa for two days, the Canadian Agricultural Outlook Conference. Not one mention was made at that conference by any farm leader-and practically all of them from all over Canada were there-about Canfarm. I say Canfarm is good and so does the hon. member, but I say we did not break our agreement. The Co-op Credit Society has agreed to fund so much money and we have agreed to fund so much money. I suggest to the hon. member that he should read the agreement on the basis of which we set up Canfarm and study it. If he is still of the same opinion I would be surprised, because the credit societies, the co-operatives and the credit unions which were involved in lending them money have said, "Look, you are not in a position to show a proper return, so we will cut off financing to you." We did not say that we would cut off financing. We asked them to bring in different projections. A different projection has been brought in by Peter Hannam and some of his colleagues in Canfarm. I say this-I said it earlier today and I will say it again: out of 350,000 farmers of Canada, only 5,000 belong to Canfarm. The farm leaders, the co-ops, the huge organizations like the United Co-operatives of Ontario, the Maritime Co-operative Services, the Sask Pool, the Manitoba Pool, the Alberta Pool, the CFA and the OFA, where have they been? The only ones who really show they want to help Canfarm, the UPA in Quebec, say "Please keep it together because we might buy it ourselves and we can put 10,000 members into the organization immediately." The Ontario Federation of Agriculture has 24,000 members and they do not even have to have 50 per cent of what UPA would put into it they would have one of the most successful organizations going.
I do not have the same responsibility as farm leaders have to their people. They have a responsibility to their people to say, "This is good, this has been provided for." It is going to cost the federal government over $5 million to give this organization the kind of backing it needs to start, and it will cost us, as I said today, total involvement. Even to phase it out will have cost us nearly $6 million which we have invested in Canfarm. Where has the response come from? It is a unique service, a service that is second to none, but there has not been much sponsorship from farm organizations or from the province of Ontario or the Ontario ministry of agriculture. If their agricultural representative wanted to sponsor it, I am sure that they

also could raise up to 5,000 new members within the province of Ontario.
The hon. member mentioned the problem of farmers not having been paid for the hay they delivered to Manitoba. That was an agreement that Manitoba had made. We made an agreement to pay one-third of the cost of transportation, Manitoba would pay one-third, and the railroads would pay one-third. We did not use up the funds which we have allocated for that program because it started to rain and they did not need as much hay from Ontario as they thought they would need.
I agree with the hon. member that the Ontario farmers have really co-operated and have come forward to say, "We have so many bales of hay which we do not need, we have a big crop." And they let them have it at a very reasonable price. Some people could not believe it was being sold for as low a price as it was. They were not trying to take advantage of the bad situation which existed because people were suffering from the drought. If someone has not paid, I will contact my colleague, the provincial minister of agriculture in Manitoba, but this is the first time such a representation has been made to me. The hon. member spoke about unity in the country. One of the members last night mentioned that some people at the Outlook conference made representations to him about some of their concerns. But let me say to the hon. member that this was one of the most positive meetings we have ever had and one of the best attended. As I said, farm leaders, national, provincial and regional, were all there. There were people from the private sector, from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and from other agro-business organizations. They all said it was a very positive meeting. I cannot say they were gleeful, but they seemed to be happy about the economic position of agriculture in Canada and the programs we have established. I would challenge the hon. member to find better programs for farmers to run their own business anywhere else in the world. No other country in the world allows its farmers to run their business as we allow them to do in Canada. Sure, we have to work with the provinces, and we do have a close working relationship with them. I say to the hon. member that it is not us who are causing disunity, not us in agriculture and not us in this government. I asked him to check some things that people on the other side of the House are saying when they suggest separatism, and all that kind of thing. The hon. member will find that people in agriculture from coast to coast are willing to share those things which grow in our ground. In these working relationships and in our national marketing boards we have the real ideal of confederation and unity.

Mr. Chairman, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate the Committee of the Whole House of Commons is holding tonight on the important question of agriculture. If I may, I would also like to thank the minister and his officials for being here to help us deal with this question. Mr. Chairman, I believe that when we talk about
Supply
agriculture, we are talking about life. If we were not so fortunate as to have such efficient farmers and agricultural producers in Canada, I believe that the well-being of every one of us would be affected.
The Department of Agriculture has always, but more particularly over the last few years, tried to provide Canadian farmers with programs geared to their needs and conducive to outstanding performance. It is because of the effectiveness of government programs that producers have been able to achieve record productions. During the seventies, agricultural cash incomes have increased tremendously as net farming income went from slightly over $1 billion in 1970 up to $4.1 billion in 1979.
Moreover, Canadian agricultural industries have become among the most effective and productive in the world. It has already been pointed out that Canada only has 3 per cent of the world's farm lands but this point should be emphasized over again. In spite of this, Canada is one of the major food growers in the world, producing 6 per cent of the wheat and barley, 12 per cent of the oats, 17 per cent of the milk, and 2 per cent of all meat and dairy products. In addition Canada exports over 70 per cent of its grain, which is the highest proportion in the world. Between 1975 and 1978, the productivity of farmers was nearly twice that of the other industries. In short, our farming community should be the envy of everyone both in Canada and abroad.
Mr. Chairman, the constituency that I represent, Rimouski-Temiscouata, is essentially rural. In my riding, farmers make every effort to improve their crops to meet the most stringent standards of Agriculture Canada. Some producers carry out their own experiments through Agriculture Canada special programs. For instance, a farming co-operative has been created in Saint-Benoit de Packington, in the Temiscouata area, for growing cauliflower and Chinese lettuce, and this program is very successful. I believe that it is through programs of this type that regional agriculture, if I may use this expression, will be able to develop in harmony with its environment.
I would not want to leave the House with the impression that I am an expert in this field; I am not, even though 1 was raised on a farm. My father was a farmer for 50 years and lived through all the plights the milk industry had to suffer from 1940 up to the present days when pasteurization and sophisticated milking methods have become common practices. In view of the significant progress accomplished in farming, especially on dairy farms, I wish to congratulate the department and the Minister of Agriculture for the personalized assistance they have extended to dairy producers.
We live in a part of the country with wide temperature ranges and I heard from the committee on agriculture that the research service was doing extremely important experiments to develop crops that might thrive in colder climates like the one prevailing in my area, for instance. So, I am anxious to see

the results of those studies so that they can be implemented in the part of the country where I live.
For almost two days I have heard many members on both sides of the Elouse. In spite of the remarks by the former minister of finance who said we are too eager to praise our minister, I think that if I had a bouquet or awards to give I would give them to our farmers. In fact, over the last few years, farmers have made use of programs which had been especially developed to meet their needs and which have proved very beneficial to them and to all of us. I think we should now go one step further as producers have demonstrated that they had the ability and the imagination to adapt to technological changes, and with very limited means to deal with the serious problem of energy cost. For example, in our area we are considering a quite revolutionary system to heat greenhouses and I will be pleased to tell hon. members more about it as soon as it is further developed. This means our farmers are not lacking energy or good will, they really are hard-working people.
I remember, Mr. Speaker, that at the time of the Speech from the Throne the government had announced its intention to lay the emphasis on assistance to farmers for the development of sectors that are thriving and new ones that could be added.
As far as the creation of a Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation is concerned, I will quote a passage from the Speech from the Throne dealing with the development of our economic potential. It reads:
Food and agriculture are going to be increasingly important to the Canadian economy in the 1980s. To further strengthen the industry, my government plans to create a Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation to expand markets for Canadian producers.
As I said a while ago, I think our producers have shown that they can develop products to meet the needs of both the domestic and the world market. Considering what goes on elsewhere in the world, I think a country like Canada is comparatively very wealthy, that it has great potential despite the poverty which is quite insignificant compared to the poverty of other people in the world when one considers that some countries have to put up with drought, with many evils, not to mention those countries that are at war, countries where the climate makes it impossible to produce foodstuff. I think it is all the more important that Canada develop internationally, that it produces new commodities for the world community. I feel that this task should belong to Agriculture Canada. The policies and programs developed by Agriculture Canada must be implemented in order to meet the needs of Canadian consumers. Producers should be urged to be selective and to be more efficient in food production.
I think Agriculture Canada should launch a worldwide campaign to promote food products made in Canada. It seems to me that the Department of Agriculture holds the pole position to travel to world areas experiencing the worse difficulties in food production so that the Canadian farmer could adjust to the world demand.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I am expecting too much but I think I would like to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) about that to know how his department explored this possibility, if it ever was considered. The establishment of such an agency was proposed in the Speech from the Throne. I think he should have some ideas about that. And I particularly would like to know which products could be offered throughout the world as Canadian products to provide as much as possible for their needs, if the production of certain products in certain regions of Canada was ever contemplated by his department and in that connection if a thought was given to products which could be made in eastern Quebec, in the lower St. Lawrence region where I live, to help Canada sell its food products to the world. I am waiting for the minister's answer.

The hon. member asks questions about the proposed Canadian agriculture export corporation. There are many things in which we are proficient in Canada. I feel we can compete efficiently with nearly any country in the world. We do not intend to compete with the Canadian Dairy Commission or the Canadian Wheat Board. But any of the products in the areas of poultry and pork production, and horticulture, areas in which we have efficiency or proficiency, whatever you want to call it, will be the areas where we shall be gearing up our concentrated efforts toward improving our exports. We intend to work very closely with the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission. Whenever the Minister of Agriculture goes abroad, or any member of the cabinet as far as that goes, we do not feel there should ever be a chance that someone should ask him or her, what products we have for sale in Canada, what products we can supply to the customer in some other part of the world. We believe that those products that were at possibly 75 per cent of efficiency at the present time could be put on long-term contracts and create 100 per cent to 110 per cent of production efficiency. We certainly do not intend to put Canagrex into a position where they would be signing up short-term contracts, contracts only when we have surpluses to sell. We must realize that many people in the world eat all the time, not just when we have a surplus. But if we could gear up our production from 75 per cent to 110 per cent efficiency, higher than it has ever been in some areas, that would mean benefits for labour, industry, the building trades, processors, the transportation system, our balance of trade and also for consumers. It would be of benefit because we would reach the peak of efficiency in those production entities, in particular in the poultry area where we are using the cost-price formula. It would be of benefit to them because it is build into their cost-price formula, and when they reach efficiency they do not get more, they agree to take less. When production per unit costs less, they agree to pass on the savings to the consumer of that product. The Canadian Egg Marketing Agency, the Canadian Broiler Marketing Agency,

Earlier today the hon. member for Roberval asked about women in agriculture. I think it would be interesting if I put on record the names of some of those women who are involved in Canadian agriculture. For the first time in history we now have a woman director of the Farm Credit Corporation. She is Mrs. Carol Teichrob, from Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and she is at the present time a director of the Canadian Turkey Marketing Agency. She is also the director of a small poultry processing plant and reeve of a huge township in Saskatchewan. With respect to the Canadian Dairy Commission Advisory Committee we have Mrs. Victoria Billingsley. She is a consumer representative from the Consumers' Association of Canada but we put her on the Canadian Dairy Commission Advisory Committee. Denise Van Breda, from southern Ontario, who is a tobacco farmer, a very successful farmer in her own right, is on the Agriculture Stabilization Board Advisory Committee. On the National Farm Products Marketing Council we have June Menzies as chairperson and Maryon Brechin as counsellor. June Friessen, a director from Winnipeg, is on the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency. Lynn Hoffman is also a director of that agency. I come back to Carol Teichrob from Saskatoon who is on the Canadian Turkey Marketing Agency. John Wise, the former minister of agriculture, appointed Brenda McIntosh to the FCC Advisory Board. In my own office I have Linda Clifford from Wilkie, Saskatchewan, who is the manager of my regional office in Regina, and is a special assistant. Mr. Chairman, I think 1 can help the minister by adding some information to what was said by the hon. member for Rimouski. My intervention does not require the minister to take any notes as he already knows what I am about to say. It is merely a question of reminding him that there are still problems in front of the Department of Agriculture.
We heard during the debate yesterday and today of the tremendous growth in farm income in Canada over the past two decades. No industry in Canada on a percentage basis has increased productivity so dramatically as agriculture. Until a few years ago the rate was 7 per cent a year compared to about a 2 per cent or 3 per cent for other industries in Canada. If the gross income for agriculture in 1980 is over $15 billion, I predict that without using any more land for production than is in use now and without too many drastic changes in technology, this same land area will be producing double the value

of its present production by the end of the century through more intensive use.
My subject tonight will be the land which exists around this good land, the so-called marginal land on which farmers have had a hard time making a living. If one takes the older provinces-the maritimes, Quebec and Ontario-one will find that more farmland has been abandoned in those provinces than is now being cultivated. My remarks will attempt to answer the type of questions posed by the hon. member for Rimouski. Her county is representative of two or three times more acreage of that type of marginal land in Canada than there is in the so-called currently cultivated acreage.
The demand for energy in the world today has given the farmer in every province of Canada an opportunity which he would never have dreamed of 15 years ago. This knowledge is not new. It is known by our research people in every department in Ottawa interested in research. It is known by our provincial research departments and by industry. But the fact is we have not used this technology and this research information on the ground that as long as there is oil we do not need to take energy from another source.
As long as we continue to use oil in Canada and the United States we delay a little longer the move toward this new technology. Fortunately, in the farm areas of Canada there is available at present prices of oil and competing energy sources a whole series of low grade technologies which lend themselves to farm use and utilization at a price competitive with other forms of energy at the present time. This competitive ability will increase each time oil prices rise. As I said before, these technologies which are coming on and which, in some cases, are here now, are not new.
One of the oldest technologies on the farm is the utilization of wind. No one will pretend that the utilization of wind energy in Canada will provide a large percentage of our total energy requirements, but it can, with the present techniques and with the present prices of competing fuels, provide about 3 per cent or 4 per cent of our energy requirements. Our scientists have produced new types of windmills, but when put to the test of economics, power derived from them is still more expensive than power bought from the ordinary electrical system. Therefore, there is no great urgency in pushing farmers into doing something which does not have an immediate economic advantage.
However, following the wind conference in Regina three years ago, farmers had figured out answers which scientists had not been able to figure out. At that conference under the auspices of Canadian Plains, University of Regina section, they had figured out how to harness the power of high speed wind. All models to date could only operate under winds as high as 25 miles an hour because under higher winds they would fall apart or the generators would burn out. The farmers applied their haywire philosophy and know-how and came up with an answer so simple that one wonders why it was not thought of 30 years ago.
To give an idea of what I mean, if the wind is blowing at ten miles an hour and it produces one kilowatt of electricity per
hour, then at 20 mph one might expect that the power produced would be two kilowatts. But because of the peculiar momentum principles of wind power, which increases at the cube of the differences of speed, and since 20 miles an hour is twice ten we therefore get two times two times two, or eight times as much power out of a 20-mile-an-hour wind as out of a ten mile-an-hour wind. In other words, eight kilowatts. If the wind velocity is 30 miles an hour, we get 27 times the power and if it is 40 miles an hour we get 64 times as much power.
That technology is presently on the way to being patented. I know that in the research section of the Department of Agriculture, which is as good as any research section in the world, they have never accepted the principle that it is their responsibility to get information out to the farmers. It believes that this is the function of the provinces, as part of the agreement of 1887. I say it is their duty, because of the failure of the provinces to properly educate farmers as to new technologies to find ways and means in co-operation with the provinces to get their information out.
Another example is heat pumps which have been used in North America for 60 years. Women know the heat pump as a refrigerator which takes the heat out of the food and dumps it on the floor. A heat pump which is used for heating a home or a barn simply takes the heat out of the air outside, even at 30 below, and heats the house or the barn. Or better, still, one should take the heat out of a well or a dugout, the local stream or even the ground. With the free heat of the sun taken from the ground, for example, one can reduce the present cost of energy by 75 per cent. All this knowledge is known but it has been resisted to the last ditch by power corporations and researchers who do not want to face reality. Fortunately this is all changing. The final decision will be made on the economics of the matter. In the last two or three years research on heat pumps to take heat from out of the ground and out of the water has demonstrated that we can save 75 per cent in spite of our climate.
The one thing that is missing of course is the capital to shift into this new technology. Without going into it in detail, it costs $3,000 or $4,000 to shift over to heat pumps which would allow a farmer to keep his dairy barn or beef barn at a constant temperature over summer and winter if it is properly ventilated. The saving in the case of larger buildings can rise as high as ten to one.
I am making my point loud and clear to the minister. We have just finished putting a budget through this Parliament which granted substantial sums of money to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to investigate new forms of low grade technology and transference of heat. The department was asked to set up demonstration programs. The only fault with that proposal is that the department does not have the personnel to deliver the programs. Several other departments do, however. Canada Mortgage and Housing has the capacity to deliver that program as has the Department of Agriculture.
December 10, 1980

Anything that reduces the cost of farming should be of interest to the Department of Agriculture.
The minister knows that in his department there is a small group of men very knowledgeable in the field of renewable energy. Other departments also have such small groups of experts but only the Department of Agriculture has the manpower at this time to deliver the service in rural areas.
Yesterday, mention was made of an organization that is one of the proudest arms of the Department of Agriculture, the PFRA or Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which covered parts of four or five provinces in the west. That organization was taken away from the Department of Agriculture about 15 years ago and transferred to the Department of the Environment, as 1 think it then was.
Those PFRA engineers are competent to design and build the biggest dam in the world, and they have done it, Mr. Chairman, but today they sit idle in Regina waiting for their pensions because they are not in the right department. The Department of Agriculture could find lots of work for them, particularly on this heat pump problem. Engineers who design dynamos and everything else for power plants could certainly design a simple heat pump made of a compressor, two coils and an electrical gadget to turn it on and off. Every woman understands her 'fridge'. Engineers understand the heat pump.
The men 1 mention would be glad to do what they did before-go out and teach farmers how to engineer a dugout system, how to put in tree plantations, how to build dams and irrigation projects. They should have a chance in their retiring years to get back to work for agriculture. I know the minister wants them back. Now is the time to bring them back to work on this program with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources for demonstration projects on energy savings. The technology is available and there is the know-how and the personnel in the Department of Agriculture to deliver the service.
This would not make Treasury Board or the Department of Finance mad, Mr. Chairman. PFRA should be returned to the Department of Agriculture and its people should go down to Rimouski and every other part of Canada that has been decimated for 50 years because of lack of knowledge as to the use of that type of soil and that type of forest capacity.
1 know the minister expects me to speak about another subject which I used to call biomass. Everybody laughed when I first brought it up. The minister picked up the term and found it to be a good way of swearing without anyone knowing what it meant. Mr. Chairman, biomass is simply rotten material. When we die, our bodies go into the ground or into the atmosphere. Every tree dies and every plant dies-every piece of grass dies. We all end the same way, as molecules of this or molecules of that. The hydrocarbon components get trapped some place and that is the basic gas, the basic oil, the basic coal, the basic diamond. Why wait for several billions of years for that to happen? A lot of us would like to be used some time reasonably close to our death. Let us get this rotten material to work, Mr. Chairman. Just the ordinary amount of waste on a
Supply
farm could supply 3 per cent or 4 per cent of Canada's total energy needs.
Yesterday someone mentioned gasohol. I know the experts say the costs are marginal-$2 per gallon when the cost of power and so on is added. But, Mr. Chairman, the farmer has the waste material anyway and is soon going to have a superabundance of power produced from all the other techniques that he knows about. One of the ways he can utilize this surplus power capacity is by using up all the waste on his farm.
Gasohol is not the main value; the main value to the farmer is this utilization of waste to produce alcohol. Of course, he cannot drink it but he can put it into his tractor, into all his engines and make them last three or four times as long. That is where the economic advantages are, Mr. Chairman. Technically, if he paid himself an hourly wage he would not make money on this product. But with the economy the farmer uses, he could make money because he does not usually consider his own wages, time or the energy which he can make himself, as costs.
In the Crosbie budget, for the first time in Canada's history there was a provision to make it legal to own a still. Rejoicing went through every farm home. Some people actually thought they might be able to sneak off a quart or two. Basically, though, the farmer knew what was meant. The required bond for a miserable little still was reduced from $200,000 to $10,000. Mounted policemen were delirious with happiness because they would now know the location of all stills, as they would have to be licensed, instead of spending cold nights searching for them.
1 think the idea of gasohol should not be dropped, Mr. Chairman. In the United States, 36 states are going ahead with production. Our civil servants now know at first hand the warm reception given to the program by thousands of farmers in many states. My constituency is just across the line from North Dakota where they make their own gasohol and we sneak across the line to get it.
For heaven's sake, Mr. Chairman, let us get this back into the budget. It would not cost the government anything. The farmer would bear the cost of the still. He would accept the police coming once a year to inspect it and would gladly put up the $10,000 bond. I am sure he would also be happy to pay his wife a few dollars for sitting to watch the still because that would be deductible.
The main point of my remarks is, of course, poplar trees, Mr. Chairman. When I first came to this House nearly 23 years ago, I made the statement that more money could be made on the farms in Canada, by producing trees than grass. For this I quickly collected the nickname of "Johnny Appleseed." I did not have the relevant figures then but I have them now, thanks to scientists in the forestry section and the research section of the Ontario and B.C. governments. We have bred a poplar tree that will not only provide feed for cattle but will provide lumber, plywood, pulp, and above all, oil. Fifty per cent of dead weight in the dry form of a poplar tree is hydrocarbon. Even at present prices that would yield a farmer, if grown on so-called useless marginal land with

December 10, 1980
