Supply
drainage, about $300 per acre each year. The cost figures are available, thanks to the Ontario government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to have this opportunity to participate in this discussion on the Department of Agriculture's supplementary estimates. As one who was a farmer prior to having been elected to this chamber, I would like to take this opportunity to convey to the Minister of Agriculture my heartiest commendations for the outstanding job he has done on behalf of all of those involved in agriculture in this country.
I am especially pleased with last week's announcement by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that the Energy Supplies Allocation Board has given agriculture a priority A rating in the event of an energy shortage. As a member of the agricultural industry, I welcome this initiative since it clearly illustrates the importance of food production for us in Canada, as well as for people in other countries.
I would like to base the first part of my questions to the minister on the subject of energy as it relates to agriculture. In particular, 1 would like to know if the minister is looking ahead to the future when higher energy prices will be hitting the farmer right square in the pocketbook. In a recent report prepared by the Department of Agriculture, some estimates were set forth illustrating the impact a $1 per barrel increase in crude oil would have on farm input costs. For example, for every $1 per barrel increase in crude, the price of natural gas will rise approximately 15 cents per thousand cubic feet. This means fertilizer prices will skyrocket. Annhydrous ammonia, for example, will rise by $10.54 per tonne. For any farmer growing wheat, barley or corn-crops of great significance in my area of the province-energy costs will be of crucial importance in deciding whether or not a farmer will make any profit in the coming years.
The key here, and I would appreciate the minister's comments on this, is what alternative will the farmer have to offset this drastic increase in input costs? Will it be by substitutes or plant adaptations?
I have read many briefs, articles and proposals for substituting renewable sources of energy for non-renewables. We all seem to realize that some sort of alcohol-based fuel would be most economical if it could be produced in large quantities. The problem is neither the technology nor the materials for producing this type of fuel are available to Canadians on a large scale.
How far down the road is this technology? I do not see energy prices getting much cheaper in the future; we need to be able to move off gasoline and diesel fuel if Canadian farmers want to stay competitive in the food production industry. My question is this: can the minister give us an idea of what priority he has allocated to a renewable energy substitution program? Also, how many years will it be before this program is implemented on a significant scale?
I would like to move to another area of concern. It deals with the fruit and vegetable storage construction financial assistance program. This program, which provides government assistance to fruit and vegetable producers in constructing storage facilities, was discontinued under the previous government. After much consultation with the producers, we reintroduced it, providing $3.3 million worth of assistance to the fruit and vegetable industry in Canada.
In Lambeth, Ontario, five producers have pooled their resources to construct a storage facility for their crops. The building was officially opened on August 25 and the owners have submitted the bulk of their cancelled cheques and invoices and have provided all the proper papers and documentation. They are anxiously awaiting their cheques from the Department of Agriculture, but at present they have not received anything of the kind. Could the minister tell me what is the current status of this project in the department, and whether these people can look forward to receiving their cheques in the near future?
Another area of interest to me is the new Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation, Canagrex. We in Canada enjoyed a very good year last year in so far as agricultural exports are concerned. Canada sold a record $6.1 billion worth of food and agricultural products abroad last year, leaving us with a healthy trade surplus of $1.4 billion. This is very commendable and indicative of the fact that when provided with the proper environment in which to produce their commodities, Canadian farmers are more than equal to the task.
Nonetheless, I feel we can improve this record. I, for one, am of the opinion that Canada can become the world leader in the international marketing of many commodities. I would like to have the minister's comments on how this could be achieved under Canagrex. I would recommend that Canagrex's board of directors be comprised mainly, if not entirely, of farmers. As far as I am concerned, no one knows the farming business as well as farmers themselves.
I would also like to know what the status of Canfarm is at present. I know my hon. colleague from Guelph discussed this matter in some detail. Canfarm offers a unique opportunity for Canadian farmers to receive expert advice and assistance. It would certainly be a substantial loss if it had to be disbanded. Would the minister tell us what he intends to do with respect to this matter?
I would like to be brief on my last topic so as to give the minister a chance to respond to my questions. However, before I finish, I would like to comment on an aspect which will, if not soon corrected, cause a severe problem for Canada in the coming decades. As I see it from here, the Department of Agriculture is not receiving the amount of moneys needed for it to achieve its maximum potential. I am not trying to say that the department is squandering its present allocations or that it is not running a tight ship. When one considers what we have done with what we have at our disposal, I cannot be anything but impressed. However, I am truly alarmed when I look at
December 10, 1980

the estimates and find that we are allocating only 1.3 per cent of our total federal expenditures to the Department of Agriculture. Compared to last year, this represents a 20 per cent cut.
Compare the Department of Agriculture's budget with that of Knowlton Nash and the boys down at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It gives one an idea of how badly off agriculture really is. In terms of employees, the CBC has 11,861 compared to 10,110 as projected for March 31, 1981. This year the agriculture departmental budget was increased by less than one per cent while CBC received a 10 per cent increase. Presently, the CBC's budget is approximately $577 million compared to $748 million for Agriculture Canada. The CBC budget is over 75 per cent of that of Agriculture Canada. Where are our priorities?
These figures are proof that the Ministry of Agriculture is not getting its fair share. I can think of no other federal department that took a 20 per cent reduction in expenditures from last year. I want everyone to wake up and remember that it was agriculture that put Canada on the map. I refuse to stand by and see the Department of Agriculture, which has in the past demonstrated its vital importance to Canada's wellbeing, receive second-class status at a time when so many people are predicting a worldwide food shortage by the end of the century. We must lay the groundwork now to prepare for the crisis ahead. I cannot see how it can be accomplished while agriculture sustains a 20 per cent cutback in revenues. 1 ask the minister, therefore, to convince his cabinet colleagues that agriculture needs more revenues to enable Canada to maintain its prestigious international position in this most important sector.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member mentioned how good the cold storage program is. He expressed concern about a group in his constituency who are waiting for a cheque. I am not aware why they have not received it. Nobody has said anything to me for some time about that organization. The hon. member made lots of representations when they were first applying for assistance under the government assistance program where we paid up to one-third of the cost of the structure with a maximum contribution of $500,000. I will have to do some checking to see if I can find out where it is for the hon. member.
He asked about Canagrex and how it can increase agricultural exports. Canagrex can do a tremendous job if it is given the opportunity. There are many small businesses and many small operations in Canada able to take advantage of export markets which can be made available to them if someone is there to back them. In many other countries of the world governments are offering all kinds of opportunities to that kind of production. It makes it very difficult for Canadian farmers to compete because there are no avenues for them to take in order to trade in other parts of the world.
The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex used figures the other day suggesting we could increase our agricultural exports by $2 billion or $3 billion in the first year of operation.
Supply
I do not think he is being too liberal when he suggests that. I think he is being very realistic. As far as that goes, he may be a little conservative when using those figures.
People come to our office about the products they wish to buy, as happened last week, and speak not in terms of $100 million, not $200 million; there is a potential of $500 million worth of new agricultural business for the year 1981. If we move quickly we can take part in that. They want to deal with the Minister of Agriculture and the government. They want to get rid of the multinationals and the people who are only in the trading business to make money. I say there is room for those people in the trading business who are willing to accept a decent profit for what they do. That is the kind of trading we want. We want to become involved with those countries producing products we cannot produce in Canada, and products we are producing in Canada which they cannot produce with as much efficiency or proficiency. Those are the areas we will be moving into.
Canfarm is a good thing. It has cost us millions of dollars since its inception but has not taken off with farmers the way it should have. When one thinks about it, only 5,000 farm members in Canada belong to Canfarm. I spoke earlier of the lack of support it has received from farm organizations and the provincial governments; it has received by far the largest amount of support from the federal government and the federal ministry. If they can find some way to come up with solutions in the next few days and if they want to work together, we will work with them to save Canfarm.
The hon. member talks about the amount of money allotted to the Department of Agriculture. We do not have that huge a budget and I brag about the little bit of money that Agriculture Canada has. There is no doubt that I can use more money for some important programs. I agree with the hon. member that food for the system is important; it is important for the mind, it is even important for the people at the CBC because they could not operate if they did not have food. When we look at the over-all structure, the CBC does provide, from time to time, some food for the mind. Sometimes it would be better if it was not provided at all. We could do without the CBC but certainly not without the farmers of Canada. Percentagewise, the CBC is probably the highest subsidized production entity there is in Canada, but I am sure we would not want to do away with the CBC either.
Some of the most progressive farmers in Canada are those who belong to the supply-managed type of marketing boards on which 1 do not spend one penny. Their production and efficiency is probably the greatest of any production entity in Canada. There are provincial marketing boards running the same kind of system and very few federal marketing boards. In total there are 103 marketing boards in Canada. Some of the toughest marketing boards of all are in Alberta where the farmers are independent and free. They just formed another one the other day to market their potatoes. The oldest marketing boards are in the province of British Columbia. All those who market milk in Canada belong to a milk marketing board. There are many farmers marketing their products. I brag

December 10, 1980
Supply
about the efficiency of our producers and the little subsidization they do receive from the federal government or from any government. When you add up the total expenditures of the provinces and the federal government and all other expenditures by other departments which involve themselves in rural Canada, we find that out of the total provincial and federal expenditures less than 4 per cent of total expenditures goes to agriculture.
I do not believe there is another nation in the whole world that can claim to have such a healthy agricultural industry with so little money spent on it. Yes, we can use more money, for research, we could use more money for cold storage, we could use money for the veterinary college in the maritimes, we could use money for the Farm Credit Corporation, we could use money to assist communities in building community centres, we could use money for the fair boards. The Canadian Exhibition associations are always asking for more money. The main reason we are here this evening is to discuss our estimates. I understand the opposition is concerned about the spending of our money. If you notice, Mr. Chairman, almost every speaker wants us to spend more money on agriculture in Canada and not to spend less. For instance, when we consider the $46 million spent on the hog stabilization industry this year, if I had a supply-managed system I would not be spending $46 million. That $46 million would be for extra research or some other kind of agricultural programs. Spending $15 million on potato stabilization is wrong. For eight years I have not spent a penny of tax dollars on the poultry industry. It is one of the healthiest production entities of all.
Groups in Canada using provincial marketing legislation are also efficient and are not costing either the federal government or their provincial governments very much money, if any at all. If they are using a supply-managed type of system with a pricing cost formula then they are all way below the cost of inflation. They are some of the most efficient production units in Canada. I just want to say to the hon. member who talked about cold storage and that type of thing that we have some programs now put forward by the province of British Columbia involving controlled atmospheric cold storage, jacketed storage, but mostly controlled atmospheric temperature. They have a plan for a two-year program to spend $9 million on cold storage because of the benefits they have received from this program. A member of the New Democratic Party said in the House yesterday that none of these programs were new and that none of them were working. They have taken advantage of that program. At one time, British Columbia used half of our funds. Now they are in a position where they export apples to 34 countries in the world because of that program. We cannot go to British Columbia and tell the farmers that there is no federal participation in their agricultural program because of what we have done to help the food and horticultural industry there. Over half of the moneys received in British Columbia for their agricultural industry are from federal government, and if you added what DREE has put into that area it would practically match what the provincial government has spent on agriculture in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the minister, but the hon. member's time has expired.
I think it was agreed earlier today that two hon. members would share any 20 minutes given. The two hon. members who will share the next 20 minutes will be the hon. member for Portage-Marquette and the hon. member for Central Nova. Each will have ten minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the minister that farmers in this country do an excellent job of producing food. One of the ways to define a so-called developed country is to measure the amount of disposable income which is spent on food. The lower the amount of money it takes to feed a country, the more developed that country is. A low percentage of disposable income spent on food is obviously a comment on the efficiency of the farmers of a particular country. I think Canadian farmers are testimony to the fact that we in this country do an excellent job of feeding ourselves.
The minister mentioned that over the past couple of days many people have asked the government to spend more. I am not asking the government to spend more, but I would like to talk about the initial price for wheat. I think the minister knows well that the initial price is $4.25 a bushel, and since about November 15 or thereabouts, or for the past month, wheat has been selling at over $7 at both Thunder Bay and Vancouver. There is a big spread between that and the initial payment of $4.25. It seems to me that an initial price increase would be more than welcomed by many farmers in this country.
1 have heard the minister and the minister in the other place who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board in the past little while say that many producers are asking that this increase be delayed until after the new year. Provincial governments and the federal government have programs in place to assist young farmers to establish themselves and to keep family farms in existence, but many people need increases in the initial price now to pay bills before the end of the year. These are the same people for whom there are government programs in place. These programs are to help young people maintain family farms.
I have also heard it said that it would save the Canadian Wheat Board interest not to have to borrow money to make initial payments. That, to me, is a completely wrong and fallacious argument. In point of fact, the Canadian Wheat Board does not have any money. It holds money in trust for producers. The interest rate at which the Canadian Wheat Board is able to borrow is substantially less than that faced by any farmer in western Canada. Indeed, the information I have is that the Canadian Wheat Board pays interest on money it borrows at prime. Most producers who borrow money to meet commitments such as operating loans and accounts payable pay in excess of prime. It would therefore make good economic sense in my mind if the government were to increase the initial price for wheat immediately and certainly before the end of the year.
December 10, 1980

I point out further that it is not the responsibility of the Canadian Wheat Board but that of the government to set the initial price for wheat. I urge this upon the minister. I would like to hear his comments on it. I urge him to increase the initial price immediately. I see no reason why he cannot do it before Christmas or before the end of the year about which I have heard him and the minister in the Senate who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board talk.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it was the hon. member for Lisgar who asked me a question yesterday in this House with respect to increasing the initial price for wheat. I gave the hon. member a response at that time. In this respect we go by our correspondence with farmers. Our regional offices tell us that the vast majority of farmers are saying that they have sold a lot of grain this year and that they do not want any increase in initial prices until January 2. That is the response I am getting. If the hon. member for Portage-Mar-quette is receiving any other type of representation, I would like to know about it. I take it for granted that he is expressing a view from his constituency, but I have been in several constituencies in each of the grain producing provinces of western Canada which come under this jurisdiction. I have been to annual meetings and seen many hundreds of farmers, but I have yet to hear one say to me that 1 should increase the initial price. 1 am going by the response I get. I do not think there is any intention at the present time, but I will be meeting the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board tomorrow, and I will take this up with him again.
The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board has been at different meetings in western Canada yesterday and today, and he may have heard a different opinion. Grain producers may now have a different feeling from that which has been expressed to me.

Mr. Chairman, 1 have certainly been in contact with some producers who favour an increase in the initial price, before the new year. However, I wonder if the minister has spoken to very many young farmers, who certainly are experiencing cash flow problems at this particular time of the year. The end of the year is approaching, and many creditors are asking that their accounts be paid. As I have said, the Canadian Wheat Board is certainly in a position to borrow money at an interest rate which is more favourable than the rate faced by the average producer. During the first 13 weeks of the crop year the Canadian Wheat Board actually sold about three-quarters of a million tonnes of wheat more than it took in in deliveries, so as far as the cash flow position of the Canadian Wheat Board is concerned, it has sold more than it has bought, so it should not be in any trouble with respect to meeting commitments in terms of increasing the initial price. I see no reason why there could not be an immediate increase of at least $1.50 a bushel.
I think that would be reasonable. I know some people have called for a $2 increase. Interest rates have gone up in the past two successive weeks and I think they will increase tomorrow. The Bank of Canada will probably see an increase of some
Supply
three-quarters of a percentage point. This makes it all the more imperative that we try to get money into the hands of producers so that they do not have to pay this high interest rate on borrowed money. I urge the minister to consider it.
I would like to raise another issue with respect to something with which I am sure the minister is familiar. It has to do with the meat import legislation which has been tabled. Is there any possibility of getting rid of the growth factor which is in the formula for setting quotas? I know this was negotiated with respect to the GATT over a year ago. I think agreements were signed back in June of 1979. This is something which concerns us. It concerns the Americans, too, because we will be letting in more meat from offshore countries on a per capita basis- Australia and New Zealand are the two major ones-than will the Americans. This can cause problems at the American border. Back in 1976 our border was actually closed because of the amount of meat which came into the country and which displaced live cattle which went south across the line. I would like to know what plans the minister has for setting quotas under the import-export permits legislation and at what levels they will be. I think they should be announced fairly soon, certainly before the end of the year.
I have one final question. I think there is some concern that our quotas for beef were set excessively high this year. The quota was some 170 million pounds of beef. There is some concern that that is excessively high and that it will be reflected in the moving average which will be with us for a long time to come. Is there any possibility of lowering the figure we had before 1980 so that that figure will not be used to inflate the quota we allow for offshore meat for the coming years? That is what I would like to have the minister address, if he would, please.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member mentioned the meat import legislation. I feel I understand what he means when he talks about the import-export legislation. It would mean setting the quota before the end of December. There have been suggestions with respect to what that quota should be. Some have said 141 million pounds. I am sure the hon. member is aware that the oceanic countries have not filled their quota this year.
It does not appear that they will fill their quota because other countries have moved in and offered better prices. Russia has moved in and bought meat from them, so their meat prices have increased to such an extent that it is not enticing to people in Canada who have been using that meat for processing. If they can find meat in North America, they will use it, but production has gone down in Canada.
I will be discussing as soon as possible with my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the setting of a quota. There has been some suggestion from the United States-I admit that it is only a rumour and I do not find it altogether authentic-that they are talking about there not being a quota. This is what we are told by our advisers at our embassy in Washington. I am in favour of setting a figure. I

December 10, 1980
Supply
believe that the Meat Import Act is something the producers have wanted for a long time. It sets a figure so that the producers know where they are going. The hon. member wants it to be more rigid than it is, as I understand from what he said about the Meat Import Act. He wanted it not to use the population consumption factor. I do not know if we could do that. In essence, the hon. member is asking for a supply-management type of system without a supply-management system. He is asking that it be done by legislation. I would think we would get into great difficulties with our trading partners in GATT if we tried that. That is why we have gone as far with that bill as we possibly can. If the hon. member will notice, in one section of that bill in which quotas for meats are-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must interrupt the minister with regret but there was an agreement earlier this day that we should allow only ten minutes to both the questioner and the minister, and that time has expired. We now move on to the hon. member for Central Nova.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister three or four brief questions, and I hope the hon. gentleman will keep his answers short, as 1 will keep my questions.
I want to bring to his attention primarily two topics. One is the question of tax and the other is the PFRA. I believe the minister indicated in his remarks a short time ago, or left the impression, that research in his department was increasing. According to my information, in 1974 there were 3,890 man-years for research, and in 1981 there were 3,659. So it would appear that in this important area his research capability is reduced. Also, in terms of inflation I believe that the expenditures have hardly kept pace. He might refer briefly to that matter in his answer.
My first question to the minister is whether he has been making representations to his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, and possibly to the Minister of Finance, as to some way in which tax concessions could be obtained, First of all, for part-time farmers who, in my constituency at least, are having a difficult time making the transition from industrial jobs to being full-time farmers, though many of them have a very real desire and incentive to do so. Has he been exploring any possibilities which would allow more generous tax concessions so that people will be able to build up some capital for farm equipment and livestock and not necessarily be denied tax deductions because they do not show a profit for the first few years?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member spoke about a reduction in man-years. My officials are looking for the figures on man-years as quickly as they can. I was given figures some time ago and I am going by memory, but it seems to me that we did not increase our man-years by very much. However, we did increase them by 14 man-years this year. The biggest increase in expenditures took place between 1977 and 1978 when the increase was $16 million.
The next largest increase took place in 1980-81 when the increase was $13 million. Both those figures show that we were ahead of the inflation rate. They also should show that we were able to maintain our status quo in man-years. Perhaps there were no large increases, but the figures I am given here right now for the end of 1979 show that we had 3,360 planned, continuing employees on March 31, 1980; 3,360 planned and continuing employees on March 31, 1981, and 3,345 total person-years authorized. This will confuse the hon. member as it confuses me, but it shows here the figure of 3,659 for the total involvement for 1980-81. That is the figure as compared to 3,392 in 1978-79, going up to 3,359. I am taking it for granted that this is for executive, scientific, administrative, technical, administrative support, operational and research groups. Those are the figures 1 have just been handed.
Concerning the national revenue people and the representations for part-time farmers, let me say to the hon. member that 50 per cent of the farmers from the area where I live work some place else. I was one of those myself at one time. I worked in factories, and so on, when I was establishing myself in farming. I find these people do not really look at marketing as much as they should if they have seniority at a good plant or if they are teaching in a school where they have tenure. They market their product without the concern that another person whose sole livelihood was derived from farming would show. The hon. member can imagine the number of representations I receive from my own area, and I think that some way should be found. When I talk to many of the people, they sound very much involved in just writing off expenditures and establishing holdings which will be worth a lot of money in a while. They write it off as farming expenditures. That is the difficulty we have.

1 understand those problems, but I am encouraged to think that the minister is looking for ways to make things easier for those who are genuinely interested in becoming farmers, because if they can be allowed to go back to the land, they will open up jobs for others who have no desire to live that kind of life.
I want to refer now to the background documentation which the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Elgin, and I have put together in our economic development committee. There was interdepartmental consultation with the Department of the Environment, the department of federal-provincial relations, and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, with respect to the future of PFRA. I was most interested in the speech given by the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain in this regard. As the minister knows, it was only in 1969, I believe, that PFRA was taken away from Agriculture. If my information is correct, the minister made a remark or two at an agricultural task force meeting of the Canwest Foundation in Calgary not long ago, under the chairmanship of Harold Horner, indicating at least some sympathy for getting PFRA back into the Department of Agriculture. My question, in the form of a representation, is the following. I have been following the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain who rightly pointed
December 10, 1980

out the number of acres of land which have been abandoned in certain parts of this country, particularly in the maritimes, and who drew attention to the expertise that is available to PFRA-even if you are growing poplar trees, you will have to do some draining. We must remember also that the special agreement which our government brought in for eastern Ontario was largely as a result of the cessation of the ARDA program which covered part of that region. Keeping all this in mind, is the minister seriously considering-I note that there will be a major departmental review and a major initiative- making PFRA a truly national agency in the maritimes-I understand this is also a provincial responsibility-along the lines of the old maritime marshland rehabilitation act? I would be very interested in this. I do not want to go on too long but I would be interested to hear what the minister has to say about this. Would he consider such action, because his predecessor and I were looking at it seriously and we were in the process of setting up an all-party task force under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Medicine Hat?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will be able to answer the question at a later time, but right now we must go over to the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct some comments to the Minister of Agriculture through you. Agriculture has always been the number one industry in Saskatchewan where my constituency lies. Although it is somewhat overshadowed right now by other developments in the potash, uranium and heavy oil industries, in the long term agriculture will always be the number one industry in Saskatchewan. However, constituents have written to me about several concerns, and agricultural groups have made representations to the New Democratic Party about their concerns in the area of agriculture. One concern which keeps coming up is the Crowsnest rate or the statutory rate for the movement of grain. I very much fear that the federal government will deal rather harshly with farmers and predict that it will make a move to take away that statutory rate. Although some compensatory payments will be made, farmers will have to watch out in the future or they will find themselves absorbing the inflationary costs of the movement of their products.
Another area of concern is the area of energy. I was happy to hear the minister announce that the producers of food would be placed on a high priority list. I thank the minister for that consideration.
1 suppose the next area would fall under the Department of Transport rather than the Department of Agriculture. I am referring to the movement of grain. Many Saskatchewan farmers say that they must stand by the siding when the train goes by, otherwise they will not get their grain in on time. They also tell me that quite often the elevators are plugged because of the poor movement of grain in western Canada.
Another area is that of a national beef marketing board which I understand is supported by the minister. Often I
Supply
questioned why the minister would not implement such a marketing board to assist beef producers, so that they could rely upon a substantial return on their product. After raising their cattle, they should be able to expect to receive something out of it, especially when one considers the money they have invested for their herds and the time and labour they have put into the operations. If their time were counted, many farmers and ranchers would not be receiving much of a return from the beef they sell during the low points of the year.
I should like to be critical for a moment of the agricultural research stations which, through attrition over the last few years, have paved the way for plant breeders' rights to come into existence, a topic with which the New Democratic Party disagrees.
The Battlefords-Meadow Lake is a strong agricultural area within Canada. As the member of Parliament for that area I disagree with plant breeders' rights. I feel we are moving into a very dangerous area when that is taken out of the research stations and put into the hands of a large corporation. It will be gobbled up quite rapidly leaving farmers at the mercy of large corporations such as Dutch Shell, for example.
I am concerned about the number of young farmers who have written me or who contact me while I am in my constituency regarding the amount of work they are required to do off the farm, particularly in the wintertime, to subsidize their incomes. Again I am stressing that they are not receiving a fair return for their work and investment; they cannot maintain a decent standard of living. Some of the people working in lumber mills or in the mining industry are able to provide much more for their families than farmers or ranchers who are working their own land. The farmers might be working much harder, but they do not receive an adequate dollar return. Many young farmers find it necessary to work in sawmills and mines in order to subsidize their incomes. As a result, to a large extent the farms are being hurt because they are not paying the attention they should to their farming or ranching operations.
I think the agricultural industry is dying in some parts of Canada, but I am happy to say that it is not in Saskatchewan. Recently Dr. Boyd Anderson, the president of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, addressed a group of people in Medstead which is in my constituency. He pointed out that less than 8 per cent of farmers engaged in the agricultural industry in Alberta and Manitoba are under 40 years of age, and that in Saskatchewan around 25 per cent of farmers are under that age. I think this is due to some of the programs which were brought in by the Saskatchewan government, namely, the farm start program and the land bank program. It would mainly be the land bank program which enables retiring farmers to pass on their lands to their children or other direct descendants. The minister should look closely at some of these agricultural programs designed to ensure that farmers remain on the land. Food production is vital for the world. It reduces our federal and international deficit. We should try to keep some younger farmers on the farms. It

December 10,1980
Supply
should be made a viable enough operation that they can work full-time at it.
Before my time runs out, I should like to ask the minister a few questions concerning the herd maintenance program. But first of all I should like to ask a question which directly concerns the estimates. How many person-years are included in the estimates under the area of research and development for this coming year as opposed to last year? If the minister will allow me a few more minutes after answering that question, I will have some questions concerning the herd maintenance program.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member indicated that he had a question for me, but I have written down about five while he was talking. The person-years in research for 1980-81 are indicated at 3,659, which is slightly down from 1979-80 when it was 3,673 or from 1978-79 when it was 3,725. The actual number of researchers has declined, but the number of people with Ph.Ds. have increased by 14; that is, that classification of researcher. It is not very much, but it is a slight increase. We find it difficult to obtain qualified people within the limitations we are guided by. We are limited as to the amount of money we are allowed to pay them.

I did not realize 1 had asked the minister so many questions, but I would be happy to hear his answers to some of my opening comments.
I should like to ask the minister some questions about the herd maintenance program. I will ask a series of questions, sit down, and allow the minister to answer at whatever length he would like. Under the herd maintenance program, many farmers throughout Saskatchewan were designated as being outside the drought areas, even though in some areas we have substantial proof from the municipalities and private rain gauges that the rainfall within those areas was actually less than fell inside the drought area. We have been told by the minister in the House-perhaps it was not in the House, but certainly it was through correspondence from the minister's office-that these people will be dealt with. Now that cheques are going out to the people who have qualified for drought assistance in drought areas, when can we expect these other farmers and ranchers to be dealt with under the herd maintenance program?
I have a second question concerning that program. I was wondering why PMU horse operations were not included under the herd maintenance program. Would the minister consider including them, so that the people involved in PMU operations could apply through the appeal process to receive assistance?

A decision was taken on Monday of this week which recommended that people involved in PMU operations be included under this program, as well as people with herds of milking goats, and, I believe, one other group excluded from the herd maintenance program. I believe three groups have been included. Perhaps this is not tremendous, but they have
suffered hardships and we recognize that they should be included in it? What was the hon. member's other question?
When will the people outside the drought area be dealt with?

I hope that the appeal committee will be set up by the end of this week. It will be publicly announced when they get into operation, which we hope will be as soon as possible. It has taken us longer than normal because it is a new program and a new experience for us. It has taken longer to get all the ramifications out of the way. I believe about 11,000 cheques have been mailed out and that about 35,000 applications have been submitted, some of which are actually being returned to the people. So people who are outside of the area will be able to appeal those decisions. I am not saying how they will be treated. I hope it will be in a very humanitarian way because we recognize that to set that criteria with rainfall-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: 1 regret to interrupt the minister but his time is up.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to continue from where I left off a few hours ago. I would like to spend some time on the marketing structure of the country.
The free market system has been allowed to work in a way that the input into farming has affected the costs of the farmer so that his income has been reduced. In the couple of cases where we do have marketing systems-which we think are pretty good, for example, the Wheat Board-we found that the Wheat Board was not allowed to work well on the international market because of the embargo. It was not allowed to work well in the domestic market because of the feed grain policy which was established by the government. However, there are a number of other areas where the minister has mentioned marketing systems on a national basis which have and are doing a good job. For instance, he mentioned the dairy policy, broiler chickens, eggs and turkey marketing boards. However, I would like to ask the minister about the plans for hog marketing and stabilization. Is the federal government prepared to introduce a national hog marketing commission and an adequate stabilization plan. If so, when does he plan to do so?

Mr. Chairman, I am meeting the Canadian Pork Council tomorrow morning for breakfast at eight o'clock. I do not know what we will decide, or if we will decide anything. It appears the program which the provincial and federal officials have been working on has not received the kind of unanimous support which I would have liked to have seen. What I would have liked to have seen would have been participation from the producers and from the provincial governments. Some provinces are in favour of it and some are not. So it appears, unless I find out differently tomorrow, that if we were to go ahead we would have to involve the federal government and the producers. It does not appear there will be
December 10, 1980

that kind of provincial participation. It appears four provinces are ready to go ahead with programs of their own; it cannot work nationally with just four provinces. At the present time 1 just cannot see a national program working with the income assurance program we are suggesting, like the Western Grain Stabilization Program. We are not getting the kind of input from some of the provinces that we should be getting.

The Canadian Wheat Board was established to cover only the prairie areas. It might be possible for the minister to extend this kind of organization to those areas which want the stabilization and marketing board.
1 would like to ask an almost identical question with respect to beef marketing. Is the federal government prepared to introduce a national beef marketing commission and adequate stabilization for slaughter cattle? And, again, if it is to be introduced, when will that be?

Mr. Chairman, I should clarify one thing. I hope I did not leave the hon. member with the impression that we are establishing a hog marketing commission. That has not been the subject of discussion. What we are talking about is a hog stabilization type and income assurance system. This is something like the one we projected for the provinces about four years ago and at that time the only province which went ahead with it was the province of British Columbia, under the previous administration. I am tempted to recommend to the government the establishment of a beef marketing commission. Even the member who speaks so eloquently in the House on beef may be ready to accept something better than the horrible system we have for marketing beef at the present time. He has been telling us about the bad economics of that for the last five years.
No way.

We do know there is a stronger movement afoot, and I am not talking about the beef cattle. 1 am talking about the beef producers in Ontario. 1 am told they have an organization which has close to 2,000 members. Those members are very active in the promotion of a beef marketing system. They want a better system than we have at the present time.
We talked earlier about the meat import law, Mr. Chairman, and what can be done with it. Some members think we can do with the meat import law what we can do with the supply management type of marketing system. You cannot do that with the meat import law. No meat import law in the world does that.

Those of us who live in Saskatchewan do a lot of mixed farming. Our herds are small and we are not able to finance the long-term losses. Some kind of stabilization and market control, which implies some supply control, would be welcome.
My last question to the minister deals with the considerable concern expressed in the last few months as to whether Canada can meet the targets which have been expressed with
Supply
regard to production in the grain area. In Saskatoon it was recently suggested that production could be increased by the required amount and that one-quarter of that amount could be attributed to research efforts. I have a couple of questions with respect to this area before my time is up. What kind of commitment has the government made to the kind of research which is necessary to bring production up to 30 million tonnes by 1985 or later? To what extent is the government prepared to demonstrate that the results of that research will work? To what extent is the government prepared to get that research out to the farmers? Right now our present growth is about 2 per cent. To reach that target we would have to increase production by 4 per cent per year, which is not typical and which is pretty unlikely to happen. How much effort is the government willing to make in order to get it out to the farmers?

Mr. Chairman, all I can say is that if the research I am aware of in western Canada concerning grain were all applied next year you could increase production 25 per cent to 30 per cent in one year, with better fertilization, better seeds and better control of weeds. Of course, the hon. member from Regina East might not want us to do that, but by using herbicides and pesticides in a better fashion, a more conservation-minded method, we know we could do a better job.
There are many areas in which we are carrying out research. I have seen some of the projects. I visited some of the different stations this year. They show a yield which would be 20 bushels above what the average farmer would be producing just with new kinds of conservation, soil conservation and the use of the other commodities 1 have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate this evening because my constituency is half urban and half rural and especially because agriculture in my area is represented by the dairy industry. 1 thought my comments would relate mostly to the dairy industry, but the previous speakers have discussed it remarkably well and have emphasized every pertinent point.
I would like to refer to an incident which will remind some of us a time when the dairy industry was experiencing some problems. A great many people had marched on Ottawa. The minister, 1 and others had been generously showered with free dairy products. We all know now that times have changed since those people had come to criticize the dairy policy, especially your marketing. 1 would like to add that the policies of the Department of Agriculture, especially as regards marketing, are well considered and devised. However, considering the approach to marketing, there will always be some people to criticize any policy, especially marketing, and when every means is taken to destroy it I think that eventually something comes out of it. Still I can assure you that things have

December 10, 1980
Supply
changed. I received a letter from some farmers on November 19 and it reads as follows:
The federal government has recently undertaken an interdepartmental survey of the dairy policy in Canada. That initiative is taken before the government has renewed its long-term commitment to a dairy policy; usually the commitments of the government should now be known. The Dairy Farmers of Canada wish to remind the government that the milk industry is of crucial importance to the Canadian economy and that it must be considered as an important link in the Canadian food chain.
A decision on the part of the government to reduce considerably the size of the dairy industry would have negative consequences not only for milk producers but also for the secondary industry as well as Canadian consumers.
We are presenting you with this short document setting forth the views of the Dairy Farmers of Canada regarding the dairy policy. Our administrators want to stress among other things the importance within the framework of the federal government's commitment, of the revision of the production cost indexation formula and the continuation of the direct subsidy designed to prevent an excessive rise in the prices of the dairy products thereby helping Canadian consumers.
We hope that this short statement will enable you to recognize the importance of the dairy industry's role in the Canadian economy because it enables many rural and urban communities to survive. This issue is of primary importance to Quebec since milk production is the cornerstone of its agriculture and that of the food product industry of that province.
Moreover, some 50 per cent of the volume required on the domestic market is produced in Quebec.
We trust, sir, that you will read with special interest the document which we are sending to you and that you will make sure that the decisions made by the various levels of government reflect the positions expressed in this document by the representatives of the Canada and Quebec dairy industries.
The Canadian Dairy Commission administers the federal subsidy and milk prices stabilization program while the establishment of quotas-and 1 stress his-and the collecting of levies are the responsibility of dairy producers associations and provincial organizations. Mr. Chairman, I wanted to read this letter into the record because I wanted to prove that it is not the marketing of the Department of Agriculture, together with the Canadian Dairy Commission which is not good. The same people who not so long ago criticized this policy and the marketing system would not accept any change made by the Minister of Agriculture under any circumstances. As I said, my remarks concerning the dairy industry will be limited to these, because my colleagues who have dealt with the government's dairy policy have built a very strong case.
I should like to mention that some of the programs which the Minister of Agriculture has implemented on behalf of the Canadian government have demonstrated that we can provide Canadian farmers with well planned long-term assistance. I should like to explain what the federal Minister of Agriculture means when he talks about long-term planning in agriculture.
1 have here a news release, dated November 14, 1980, from the Minister of Agriculture, and I quote:
The Minister of Agriculture today announced a program to assist in transporting about 10,500 tonnes of Ontario juice apples to processors in Quebec and Nova Scotia.
This year's Ontario processing apple crop, estimated at 75,000 tonnes, is about 10,500 tonnes more than the Ontario apple juice industry needs, Mr. Whelan said.
However, apple processors in Quebec and Nova Scotia are experiencing a shortage of juice apples in their areas.
The federal government will pay two-thirds, about $375,000, of the cost of transporting the apples. Eastern processors will pay the remainder of the transportation cost.
I believe this program will help Ontario apple producers dispose of their surplus crop, and it will help processors in Quebec and Nova Scotia meet their need for juice apples.
Mr. Chairman, all those programs the Minister of Agriculture offers us will certainly help Canadian agriculture to develop.
Allow me to quote another announcement the Minister of Agriculture kindly made to the farmers of Canada, and especially those of Quebec:
-May 30, 1980-Today, the Minister of Agriculture announced that a cheque for $5 million was sent the Quebec minister of agriculture, fisheries and food, Mr. Jean Garon, under the Feed Freight Equalization Program.
As a result of the very high demand for assistance from the farmers, the $6.7 million earmarked annually by the federal government for that program have been used up. We are therefore releasing funds previously intended for the coming fiscal year (1980-81) to meet the requests of the farmers during the fiscal year 1979-80. The Feed Freight Equalization Program was set up in 1978 to help increase the production and storage of feed in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia.
Those funds will also help make up for the cancellation of the Feed Freight program that applied to feed coming from the prairies. Under the agreement reached with Quebec, the federal government will pay $33.5 million over a period ending in 1983. That program is administered wholly by the provincial government; it extends four types of financial assistance: for the storage of feed and cereal on the farm; for the purchase of crop equipment; for the improvement of feed conservation; and for the production of seed grains. The program has already been of considerable assistance to Quebec farmers in helping them meet their feed requirements. The program also fits in well with the over-all strategy of the province for agricultural development.
Mr. Chairman, that, to my mind, is another proof that the Minister of Agriculture wants to set up a planning program to help Canadian farmers stay in agriculture while helping to ensure a viable agricultural sector. Farmers are relatively large consumers of energy, and it was felt that they should be helped.
The Minister of Agriculture said that he was very pleased with the announcement of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board, saying that the primary sectors of production and processing of essential perishable goods will be in category A and that in a national crisis, they would have priority in the allocation of oil products.
According to the oil products allocation program of the board, the various uses for oil are broken down into different categories. Category A is composed of all uses concerning the health, welfare and security of Canadians.
The minister observed that these priorities were in line with the position he took with his provincial colleagues during the meeting on energy matters they held in Brandon, last October.
He also indicated that producers and processors of essential perishable goods will be allocated the maximum amount of
December 10, 1980

fuel in an emergency. Therefore the supply of Canadians in essential goods will not be interrupted.
In consultation with Agriculture Canada, the board will determine what sectors of the agricultural and food industry will be classified in the A and B categories. The minister can rest assured that Canadian farmers did not expect any less from him than this statement giving them the guarantee that in the event of an energy crisis, they will be able to maintain their supplies of oil, which is an essential product for the Canadian agriculture.
I would like to demonstrate once again that the present Minister of Agriculture makes every effort humanly possible to help Canadian farmers. Recently he went to China to discuss market possibilities with Chinese officials. Canada-China co-operation has had a significant boost today with the signature of an agreement between the two countries. The agreement signed by Agriculture Canada and the Chinese ministries of agriculture, state farms and land rehabilitation calls for closer co-operation between our countries in several areas, such as joint projects, information and material exchanges, scientific visits and commercial contacts.
The first activity organized under this agreement is a visit by a Chinese delegation which will come to study our agricultural legislation. This is the first time such an agreement is signed between a Canadian department and its Chinese counterpart. The implementation of this agreement will be subject to yearly consultations between the Canadian and Chinese agriculture departments. The minister announced the signing of this agreement during a press conference in Peking after a meeting with the deputy prime minister and the chairman of the Chinese Agriculture Commission.
Mr. Chairman, we should be happy that the Deparment of Agriculture has taken this approach and these initiatives to help our producers gain access to domestic markets and entertain the possibility of reaching world markets. Under this agreement, there are some projects that could be implemented as early as 1980-81, for example, a joint research program on route management, the setting up of a model ranch in northeastern China, various seminar-conferences with assorted activities and possibly study and work exchanges. The Minister of Agriculture was the first in that capacity to visit China.
1 want to emphasize how important it is for us that our farms are family operations in 95 per cent of cases and that the minister has opted for an agricultural policy that favours such types of operation. Take, for example, the loan policy of the Farm Credit Corporation. Last year 98 per cent of loans were granted to unincorporated family operations, and most of the incorporated operations were controlled by farmers. The stabilization program under the Agricultural Stabilization Act as well as the Western Grain Stabilization Act set the minimum and maximum amounts to ensure that the bulk of the money goes to family type farms rather than farm corporations. Also, agricultural research attempts to find ways to
Supply
make the family farm more profitable. In the short term, that will boost farm income and in the longer term it will make it possible for Canadian farmers to compete with foreign farmers and to ensure the viability of their operation.
Mr. Chairman, I agree with the minister's position that we must do our utmost to ensure that farms continue to be operated by families. Mr. Minister, I share your concern over the fact that the number of such operations has decreased continually in the last 20 years as it went from 480,000 in 1961 to 340,000 in 1976, yet I do think that the worst is behind us. In other words there are fewer farmers in Canada. I dare hope that the number of commercial farms in Canada is levelling off and I say we have everything we need to increase our production.
With more intensive farming methods there could even be more farms. World population is growing at the rate of about 2 per cent a year. We have the land, the farmers and the required knowledge to produce more food. Economic development did contribute to raise the standard of living in several Third World countries. New markets are now available for Canadian dairy products and meat. There are hundreds of marketing opportunities for a whole range of Canadian products.
Canadian agricultural production, besides benefitting from tremendous export possibilities, can also develop its domestic markets. Do hon. members know that more than half of the $4.7 billion of food imported in Canada last year were competing directly with food we produce or could produce right here in Canada? Therefore we must try harder to make consumers replace at least some imports with food produced in Canada. But that will require the co-operation of farmers, processors, federal and provincial governments. The Minister of Agriculture is already initiating a certain number of projects.
Mr. Chairman, once again I am extremely happy to have taken part in this debate and in conclusion I should like to urge the Minister of Agriculture and his team to keep on giving farmers such good programs. Keep up the good work, Mr. Minister. We like you just the way you are.

I am sure the minister is aware that the Canadian livestock industry provides about 50 per cent of the farm cash receipts in this country. He may not be aware that only 20 per cent of the research dollar is spent in this area and only 6 per cent of this 20 per cent is related directly to research in diseases of livestock.
Tonight I would like to talk for a moment about a research laboratory in Saskatoon with which I think the minister is familiar, the Veterinary Infectious Disease Organization, VIDO. Some years back the farm community and veterinarians in the country recognized this gap in research. They were

December 10, 1980
Supply
able to mobilize funds and build a $4 million laboratory in Saskatoon on the campus of the University of Saskatchewan. It is not part of the university. It is simply located there because it is close to the college of veterinary medicine, and the university donated the five acres of land on which the laboratory is located. The board of directors is made up of 12 members, five of them producers representing all the main producer groups. Two are members of the University of Saskatchewan and the three are from government, one each from the government of Alberta, the government of Saskatchewan and the federal government. There are also two businessmen on the board.
The producers select the diseases to be researched. They are looking for diseases which cause great economic loss to the producers of Canada. The first one they picked was neo-natal diarrhoea in calves, or calf scours. The minister is probably aware that this laboratory has done some outstanding work. It made a major breakthrough two years ago and has now licensed to Connaught Laboratories a vaccine which is very efficient in preventing scours caused by E-coli in calves.
This vaccine is now licensed in the United States. It is hoped to have it licensed in South America and Europe soon. There will be a good dollar return to Canada from sales of this vaccine.
It is interesting to look where the funding came from for this laboratory. Over 60 producer groups from across Canada have put in money. For example, the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency put in $50,000, the Canadian Turkey Marketing Agency, $200,000 and the Alberta Cattle Commission $90,000. I could read on and on. The government of Alberta put in almost $2 million and the government of Saskatchewan over $1 million. The British Columbia government contributed, as did the government of Manitoba. The drug companies put in about $200,000 and the Devonian Group of Charitable Foundations, located in Calgary, put in approximately $3.5 million.
To date about $8,800,000 has been donated by these various groups along with dozens and dozens of individual producers. It is interesting to note that over the seven-year period this lab has been in existence the federal government has donated $43,000 to this institution, which is less than one-half of one per cent of total capital expenditures and operating costs to date.
The director, Dr. Chris Bigland, a world famous figure, was recently selected by the Ontario Veterinary Association for his outstanding contribution to the science and given an award. I think the last person to get this award was James Herriot. It is an extremely efficient, well run and good research laboratory.
The director has been to Ottawa about 25 times to solicit funds for this laboratory. These trips have cost from $30,000 to $50,000. He has met with Agriculture Canada, the Science Council, the Ministry of State for Science and Technology, the Ministry of Trade and Commerce, the NRC, NSERC, IDRC, EDP, the food and drug directorate of health and welfare, MRC, Canada Manpower and DREE. He has presented three
briefs to the minister, one in 1975, one in 1978 and one in 1979.
My question to the minister is this: what is wrong with the federal government? Why can we not afford to put some meaningful funds into this laboratory? It is doing an outstanding job. They are also working on poultry and swine diseases and have launched a major drive on shipping fever in cattle.
I should also add they are getting royalties from Connaught Laboratories, but this vaccine they came up with is not patentable. They will probably lose the lead on that in two or three years, and the money coming in from the royalties will be diffused by other companies getting into the business. I ask the minister to comment on the fact that only 6 per cent of the 20 per cent figure for research is designated in Canada for disease research in livestock and on the fact that the federal government has seen fit so far to only put a piddling amount into this laboratory.

Mr. Chairman, I am very much aware of the laboratory and the research the hon. member is talking about. It is tremendous that somebody else is getting into research. I have the largest budget for research of any ministry in Canada. This year we are spending $155 million on research. There is nothing wrong with what is spent by governments on agricultural research. The federal government pays for 98 per cent of the research and the provinces 2 per cent.
The hon. member mentioned that the money is put in by Alberta. I think that is a tremendous thing to do with their Heritage Fund. If they would give me a couple of million bucks or a little pile of it, I would spend it on research. The hon. member for Vegreville is sitting with a very charitable look on his face as though he thinks that is a good idea. I can see this disease which causes a high mortality rate in calves being controlled by research.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat talked earlier about cattle and increasing the population. I am very much aware of what this disease causes in some areas. Going from memory, I believe we lost as much as 55 per cent of the calf crop in some areas. That was a tremendous loss.
All research done with regard to livestock is done to benefit all parts of Canada. The hon. member acknowledged that. The fact that donations have come from across Canada, including the marketing agencies, shows that they have faith in what is being done. 1 think more money should come from the private sector rather than the government sector. I would love to be able to say that I have money for them and will give it to them. We have tried to find ways to help them. We are ready to move 12 of our scientists from the laboratory in Guelph to work at the university laboratories in Saskatoon and to work in conjunction with VIDO. That is not exactly what the member for Medicine Hat said he wanted. However, I did mention VIDO when he made representations to me about agriculture research in western Canada. He was making a comparison. He said we spent more in eastern Canada than in western Canada.
I saw the hon. member at the B.C. cattlemen's annual meeting in Cranbrook. He made a representation to me there about it.
December 10, 1980

1 think this is one of the most worth-while programs there is. If they can find a cure for this disease, it will be a tremendous breakthrough. I just don't have the funds.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Agriculture referred to me in his comment. I want to point out to him that one of the reasons the province of Alberta has a heritage trust fund is because it exercises prudent financial management. If the government of which the Minister of Agriculture is a member would exercise such tight fiscal managerial controls over the funds entrusted to them, they would probably have some money to spend on some of the programs to which my colleague is referring.

speechtext: The hon. member has hardly made a point of order.

1 should like to follow the questions put forward by my colleague and try to spend more time on research and development. I will make my questions short so as to get short answers as well and perhaps cover some of the relationships between agriculture and energy. It is an increasingly important area. If the minister and his department understand this area they certainly do not seem to have been very successful in bringing forward solutions for some of the problems which are developing. From some of the answers given here, the minister seemed to indicate he felt that Agriculture Canada was indeed putting what it should into research and development. However, his own research and development branch, particularly on the basis of the comments they made in front of the alternative energy committee, is well aware their efforts are very much less than they should be. They are now getting $1.5 million to do all the research and development for energy related to agriculture for the whole country in an area where the federal government clearly should be taking leadership. Even to do the basic minimum they would need about $9 million in about 30 man-years. Would the minister comment as to whether he feels that is an appropriate level of funding and of man-years?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member mentions a figure. As early as 1974, Agriculture Canada began funding research on alternative energy for agriculture. The funds invested in contract research are now $4 million. We know that research is very important. Some of our own people point out that for every dollar invested in research a $9-return is received. We have funded over 50 per cent of all research done in Canada. Let us not forget about the amount of money we give to universities. When I first came to Ottawa we gave $26 million to the higher schools of learnings. Last year we gave well over $2 billion to the higher schools of learning and they are doing a lot of research in agriculture. We are paying 50 per cent of all administration costs in universities out of federal taxation moneys. Even the school where the hon. member received his medical education benefits; it cost us $250,000 to put him through school. That is not done for very many young farmers in any fashion or form. The veterinarians
Supply
who go through school are funded by this tremendous amount of money and we are accused of being the bad financers of the country and the mismanagers of the economy. Alberta takes 45 per cent of the revenue from the resources from under the ground and we did not contribute anything to them, we just happened to be living on top of them. If that is good management then I would like to be part of that good management. Perhaps then I could look after some of those things they want me to spend more money on such as research. I do not have the resources to draw from. It has very little to do with good management as the hon. member for Vegreville said. They do not know what to do with it. They do not know how to spread it around and make it grow.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has been very ably side-stepping my question. The point of the issue is that agriculture uses about 3 per cent of all of the total energy demand of the whole country. I am not asking him about Alberta or some other province managing its own resources or whether Quebec is looking after its hydroelectric power any better than Alberta is looking after its oil. I do not think that is relevant.
Will the minister provide some leadership at the national level to farmers who have problems with energy costs relating to the operation of their tractors and energy costs related to fertilizer costs. The National Energy Board tells us there is going to be an increase of $4.5 per barrel of oil per year for the next three years. That equates a cost of production going from $3.5 per acre up to about $14 per acre depending on what farmers are growing.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture came before us and presented a brief asking the federal government to provide some leadership. I am asking the minister to do three specific things and comment on whether he thinks they are appropriate for the government to do at the national level. One is to audit on-farm energy uses so that Agriculture Canada may tell farmers where they can save, where they can conserve and where they can implement proper oil substitution measures. The second is to make an on-farm assessment of what opportunities are available for different farmers to take advantage of alternate energy forms. There are many energy forms but I do not have an opportunity here today to talk about all of them. The minister is well aware of some of them. Even though he has not done anything as yet and even though Agriculture Canada has not replaced one drop of oil on farms for farmers who have to work their fields, there are many, many opportunities. They could be assessed, they could be described, and assistance could be given.
The final thing the minister could do would be to assist at government level to provide the co-operative framework for farmers to put in pilot projects on farms for things such as ethanol plants. Those are three of the things the Canadian Federation of Agriculture asked for. Will the minister tell us if he will help through Agriculture Canada to provide that kind of assistance?

Mr. Chairman, if I understand correctly, the hon. member is talking about energy conservation demonstration projects.

These are three simple things the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has asked the federal government to assist with. I do not think the minister is "with it" as far as energy is concerned. I do not think he has a concept of what energy audit is all about. There is energy in and there is energy out. That is tremendously important in understanding how to manage energy resources. Farmers have energy inputs and energy outputs and Agriculture Canada could help to determine what those are through an energy audit. Then there is an assessment function which could be undertaken; Agriculture Canada, through some of its facilities would provide an assessment of the opportunities on a particular farm scene for taking advantage of different energy forms or for substitution away from oil. This is something his government has put forward as a priority. The final thing is pilot projects. This is clearly the way we have to go-through co-operative efforts and pilot projects to make sure we get some of these alternative energy sources developed.

The hon. member has his view about my understanding of energy input and output on farms and that is his right. We have studied the energy input on farms. For instance, we have produced grain which is going to provide energy, we have assessed the amount of energy collected from the sun to produce crops and so on. We have done a lot of work on that. There is $8 million unused by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources for pilot projects and submissions have been made to them and considered by the agricultural engineering department. I think there are some 40 demonstration projects of energy conservation and new ways of creating energy in Ontario at the present time, not paid for by my department but by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources under that special fund. It is not $1.5 million; 1 believe there is $140 million in that fund for such programs. A lot of farmers are using them. The hon. member talks about the Federation of Agriculture and their farm audits. I do not know where the Canadian Federation of Agriculture got that idea. I have talked to some farmers about it and they are saying, "Are they telling me that 1 don't run an efficient operation, that I don't know how to run an efficient tractor, that I don't know how to cultivate my soil in the proper fashion?"
The whole program put forth by my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, takes in a wide sphere of things for conservation of energy and energy use.
I am just a plain ordinary farmer. I am not a highly educated person, but I know that all of the things about which the hon. member is talking are very important.
